effects.log: "And who lights the road?" he says. "The road lights itself, if enough people walk it," you say. He opens his mouth, closes it, and laughs. "Draw," he says.

choices.text: Spar with him, arts against rites

effects.log: Your arts against his rites, on a narrow landing, both of you laughing. He loses, cheerfully, and insists that the floor was tilted.

choices.text: Concede that his lamp is kinder

effects.log: He looks at you suspiciously. "That is a trap," he says. "An eastern trap." It is not, and he knows it, and he is pleased all the way up the next stair.

events.text: The floor throws you, hard, toward the open edge of the stairwell, and there is nothing to hold. Then there is: a brass lantern pole, hooked through your belt, and Wil Vael on the other end of it, both boots braced on the rail. "Got you," he says through his teeth. "Got you. Do not move. Please do not move."

choices.text: Hold still and let him pull you in

effects.log: He pulls you in, inch by inch, and sits down hard on the landing when it is done, shaking. "That," he says, "is the worst thing that has ever happened to a lamp."

choices.text: Thank him, when you can breathe

effects.log: "Do not thank me," he says. "Teach me how you fell so well. I would have broken in three places." He is still holding the pole as if you might go over again.

choices.text: Tell him he should not have risked it

effects.log: "Should not?" He looks honestly confused. "You were falling. What else is a lamp for?"

events.text: You win the floor, but in the last moment something comes at your back that you do not see. Wil Vael does. He steps into it with the lantern held high, and it strikes the brass and him together, and the light goes out for the first time since you have known him. He sits on the floor in the dark. "Ow," he says. "Somebody relight me."

choices.text: Relight his lantern with your own qi

effects.log: You hold your hand to the wick and push. It catches, a little bluer than before. He stares at it. "Now it is half yours," he says. "That cannot be undone. Good."

choices.text: Help him up and check his ribs

effects.log: They are bruised, not broken. He grumbles the whole time you check. "Lamps," he says, "are not meant to be shields. Do not tell my family."

choices.text: Tell him he saved you

effects.log: "Did I?" He beams in the dark. "Good. I have been wanting to do that for three floors."

events.text: Wil Vael is waiting on the landing with his lantern set down and his coat brushed. He looks nervous, which you have never seen. "On my side," he says, "people who keep finding each other on the road swear a vow. Road-kin. On your side, I am told, you have an oath too: under the sky, with wine or water, as sworn kin." He holds out both stonewright's hands. "Across the seam. Both worlds. Will you?"

choices.text: Swear it, the eastern way and his way both

effects.log: You kneel facing west and he kneels facing east, and you say the old oath of sworn kin under the sky, and he says his road-vow, and you share water from his flask because there is no wine. "Kin," he says, trying the word. "Across the worlds. At the top, I will wait at the west door."

choices.text: Swear it simply, in plain words

effects.log: "Kin," you say, and he says it back, and you clasp hands over the lantern flame, and that is all. It is enough. "At the top," he says, "I will wait for you at the west door. Do not make me wait too long."

choices.text: Tell him you are not ready to swear

effects.log: He nods slowly, and picks up his lantern. "Not ready is not no," he says. "My family has a saying: the road is long, and the lamp keeps." He lights your way up the next stair, as always.

events.text: Wil Vael is on the landing again, in another life of yours, his lantern lit. He does not mention the vow. He argues about qi and lamps, as he always does, and fights beside you, and at the top of the stair he looks at you once, quickly, and away.

choices.text: Ask him to swear the vow now

effects.log: His face lights up brighter than the lantern. You kneel, east and west, and swear it, the oath of sworn kin and his road-vow, with water from his flask. "At the west door," he says. "Always."

choices.text: Climb on as friends

effects.log: Friends is a good word too. He says so himself, and means it, and lights the stair.

choices.text: Argue that lamps belong inside, again

effects.log: He is delighted. "Finally," he says. "I was getting bored."

events.text: Your sworn kin from the other sky is on the landing, lantern lit, as if he had been waiting just for you, which he has. "Kin," Wil Vael says, and grins. "The west door is still there. I checked. Shall we argue about lamps, or fight something, or both?"

choices.text: Both, as always

effects.log: You fight the floor and argue the whole way up. Neither of you wins either.

choices.text: Ask how the road is on his side

effects.log: Long, he says. The lamps are lit. People keep finding each other on it. He tells you their names.

choices.text: Let him take a blow, then take one for him

effects.log: He takes one for you; you take the next for him. "Fair," he says. "Kin keep score so they can lose it."

events.text: Brother Odo is waiting on the steps of the red hall with two cups and a jug of water, which for him is solemn. "In my order," he says, "when two people have fought side by side enough times, they swear to be kin. Every hearth of the Open Door would know your name. I would like to swear it with you. Here. Today."

choices.text: Swear kinship with Brother Odo, under both skies

effects.log: You swear it on the red lacquer steps, his way and yours: a cup of water each, a bow to the east, a bow to the west, his laughing prayer and your old oath. "Kin," he says, and laughs so hard he spills the water. "Across the seam!"

choices.text: Tell them you would rather stay friends

effects.log: Brother Odo nods, and does not ask again this life. "Friends," they say. "That is not small either."

choices.text: Ask what the vow means on their side

effects.log: They tell you: a name said at every hearth, a seat kept at every table, a door that is never barred. It is not so different from the east.

events.text: Brother Odo, your sworn kin from the other sky, is on the steps of the red hall with a pot of terrible soup. "Kin!" he booms, and hugs you so hard your ribs complain. "Every friar of the Open Door asks after you. Come, the eastern fist and the friar's fist, together."

choices.text: Fight beside your sworn kin

effects.log: He laughs the whole floor through and takes no blow meant for you that he can reach. You take the ones meant for him.

choices.text: Eat the soup, as kin must

effects.log: It is terrible. You both finish it. That is the vow, he says.

events.text: Elowen Brisk sits at the iron stair with her hawk asleep on her knee. She does not look at you when she speaks, which is how you know it matters. "Wardens swear kin," she says. "Not often. I have never. I would. With you." She pulls out her knife and cuts a strip of green cloth from her hood, and holds it out.

choices.text: Swear kinship with Elowen, under both skies

effects.log: You tie the green strip round your wrist and give her a strip of your own sleeve, and say the old oath of sworn kin under the sky, and she says three words of the Wardens' tongue. The hawk wakes up for it. "Kin," she says. Then, very quietly, "Good."

choices.text: Tell them you would rather stay friends

effects.log: Elowen nods, and does not ask again this life. "Friends," they say. "That is not small either."

choices.text: Ask what the vow means on their side

effects.log: They tell you: a name said at every hearth, a seat kept at every table, a door that is never barred. It is not so different from the east.

events.text: Your sworn kin is at the iron stair: Elowen Brisk, the green strip still round her wrist, faded. Her hawk lands on your arm before she says anything. "Kin," she says, which for her is a speech.

choices.text: Track the floor together

effects.log: She tracks, you fight. You do not need to speak at all.

choices.text: Light a fire first, as kin

effects.log: The hawk sleeps on your arm. Elowen talks, nearly a whole sentence at a time.

events.text: Mira Thistledown stands at the silver door with her holy sign in her hands. "I chose who to be," she says. "Now I would like to choose who to belong to. The Grey Sisters let us swear kin with one person in our lives. Only one. I would like it to be you, if you will have me."

choices.text: Swear kinship with Mira, under both skies

effects.log: She blesses you, and you swear the old oath of sworn kin under the sky, and the Archivist, without being asked, writes it in both your scrolls at once. "Kin," Mira says, and laughs because she is crying. "I will remember this one. I will remember this one."

choices.text: Tell them you would rather stay friends

effects.log: Mira nods, and does not ask again this life. "Friends," they say. "That is not small either."

choices.text: Ask what the vow means on their side

effects.log: They tell you: a name said at every hearth, a seat kept at every table, a door that is never barred. It is not so different from the east.

events.text: Mira Thistledown, your sworn kin, meets you at the silver door. "The Archivist shows me your scroll sometimes," she says. "Only the good parts. It says there are a lot of them." She raises her sign. "Come, kin."

choices.text: Climb the silver floor with your sworn kin

effects.log: She blesses every blow you take, and you take every blow you can for her.

choices.text: Ask what the Archivist wrote

effects.log: "Kin," she says, "in both our hands." She shows you. It is true.

events.text: Rowan Hale sets his silver storm-sign down on the cloud, which he never does. "In the Tempest Chapter," he booms, then lowers his voice, "we swear kin with the ones who stood under the storm beside us. I have stood under nine strikes with you more times than I can count. Swear with me?"

choices.text: Swear kinship with Rowan Hale, under both skies

effects.log: You swear it under the ninth drum, his storm-vow and your old oath under the sky, and the thunder answers in a voice like rain on a roof. "Kin!" he roars, and the Marshal, of all people, bows his head.

choices.text: Tell them you would rather stay friends

effects.log: Rowan Hale nods, and does not ask again this life. "Friends," they say. "That is not small either."

choices.text: Ask what the vow means on their side

effects.log: They tell you: a name said at every hearth, a seat kept at every table, a door that is never barred. It is not so different from the east.

events.text: Rowan Hale, your sworn kin, is waiting under the cloud stair, grey-bearded, booming. "Kin!" he shouts, as if you had been gone a day. "Nine strikes. Smaller. Together."

choices.text: Stand under the storm with your sworn kin

effects.log: Shoulder to shoulder. The storm finds almost nothing to hit.

choices.text: Say his prayer over him, for once

effects.log: He goes very quiet while you say it, accent and all. "Kin," he says afterwards, gruffly. "Do not do that again. Do it every time."

events.text: The ninth strike of the ninetieth floor is the worst you have ever seen, and it is coming for you, and Rowan Hale steps under it. He raises the silver storm-sign over his head and shouts his prayer into the light, and the light takes him. When it is gone he is lying on the cloud, very still, smiling, the sign still in his fist. "Smaller," he whispers. "See? Smaller." He does not speak again.

choices.text: Carry him down the Tower yourself

effects.log: You carry him down every floor, all ninety, to the gate. The Keeper sets out a cup of tea for him, and sweeps the step where you lay him, and says, "The Tower remembers him. So will the other side." Somewhere a bell you did not ring rings once.

choices.text: Keep his storm-sign, and say his prayer

effects.log: You take the sign from his hand and say his prayer over him, every sound wrong, every word meant. Thunder answers, softly, in a voice like rain on a roof. The sign is warm in every life after this.

choices.text: Stand under the rest of the storm for him

effects.log: You stand where he stood, and the rest of the storm breaks on you and finds nothing it can move. When it clears the Marshal is kneeling beside Rowan, helm off.

events.text: At the cloud stair, where a battle-priest used to wait, there is a young priest in a grey cassock you have never met, holding a silver storm-sign worn smooth. "The Tempest Chapter sent me," the young one says. "Rowan Hale's chapter. We were told: the eastern climber he died for will come. Stand beside them. Pray the storm smaller."

choices.text: Let the young priest pray

effects.log: They pray in a voice that is not like rain on a roof yet. It will be. The storm is smaller.

choices.text: Teach them how Rowan stood

effects.log: You show them the stance, shoulder to shoulder. They learn it badly, and loudly.

events.text: Tobias Wick is on the jade stair ahead of you, and he does not wait. "Sorry," he calls back, grinning, not sorry. "The orphanage has a hundred now. I need the guardian's gift more than you do. I am climbing against you, friend. Fair and square. Mostly square." He picks the lock of the jade door and is through it before you.

choices.text: Race him, fair and square

effects.log: You race him across the jade floor and the scales, and whoever wins, he laughs, and you do too. From now on you are rivals. It suits you both better than you expected.

choices.text: Let him have this one, for the hundred

effects.log: You let him take it. He knows you did, and it makes him furious, which is how you know you are rivals now and not just friends.

choices.text: Pick his pocket on the way past

effects.log: You lift his best lockpick as he passes. He finds out three floors later and howls with delight. "Rival!" he shouts down the stairwell.

events.text: A sellsword in a good grey cloak gone shabby at the hem is resting on the landing, a black heron stitched on his shoulder: House Harrow of the Blackfen, a fallen house of his sky, he tells you, with a rueful smile. "Valen Harrow. From the other gate. I climb alone and it is dull." He walks the next floor beside you, easy company. Only once, on the stair, he asks: "What does a guardian give, exactly, when you beat it?"

choices.text: Tell him what you know of the guardians' gifts

effects.log: He listens closely, nodding, and thanks you twice. He is very good company for the rest of the floor.

choices.text: Tell him the gift is the floor, not the prize

effects.log: He laughs. "Spoken like someone whose house still has a roof," he says, lightly. You both climb on.

choices.text: Ask him why he wants to know

effects.log: "Curiosity," he says, too quickly, and then, more slowly, "my house is owed a great deal." He changes the subject. He is good at that.

events.text: Valen Harrow is waiting on the landing again, with a fire lit and bread for two. He has been a good friend these floors: he watches your back, he shares his water, he laughs at the right things. Tonight a letter lies half out of his pack, sealed with a black heron. He sees you see it and does not move to hide it.

choices.text: Read the letter while he fetches water

effects.log: It is from his house. One line is underlined twice: "Bring home a guardian's gift, by any road, or do not come home." You put it back exactly as it was.

choices.text: Leave the letter alone: it is his

effects.log: You leave it. He comes back with the water and talks about the Blackfen in spring, and you like him very much.

choices.text: Ask him about his house

effects.log: "Fallen," he says. "My father sold the last of the land to pay a debt to a better house. I am all the Harrows have left to spend." He smiles. It does not reach his eyes.

events.text: Floor after floor, Valen Harrow climbs beside you, and he has saved you twice now on the stairs. Tonight he insists on taking the second watch, and the place behind you on the stair tomorrow. When you wake in the night he is sitting very still, sharpening a short knife you have never seen him use, and looking at the stair to the guardian's door.

choices.text: Pretend to sleep, and watch him

effects.log: You watch him through your lashes until dawn. He sharpens the knife and puts it in his boot, not his belt. You will remember which boot.

choices.text: Say goodbye in the morning and climb on alone

effects.log: You tell him you will climb the next floors alone. Something crosses his face, relief or regret, and then it is gone. "Of course," he says. "Good road." You do not see him again in this life.

choices.text: Thank him for the watch, and sleep

effects.log: You sleep. In the morning he is cheerful and has breakfast ready. You climb on together, toward the guardian's door.

events.text: On the last landing below the guardian's door, Valen Harrow puts a friendly hand on your shoulder, and the other hand comes out of his boot with the short knife in it. "I am sorry," he says, and means it. "My house needs the guardian's gift more than I need a friend."

choices.text: Turn before it lands: you knew which boot

effects.log: You were watching for it. You turn, and the knife goes past your ribs into the doorframe, and you have his wrist. He stares at you. "You knew," he says. "You knew, and you climbed with me anyway." You let him go down the stairs alone.

choices.text: Take the blow, and catch him at the door

effects.log: The knife finds you. Not deep. You catch his cloak at the door anyway, and he pulls free and goes through without looking back, toward a gift he will never be able to hold. Far below, the Keeper sweeps the step where you will come down, and says, "The Tower remembers that, too."

choices.text: Take the blow, and let him go

effects.log: The knife finds you, and you let him go. He goes through the guardian's door alone. Below, at the gate, the next bell is silent for him, and you hear the Keeper say, very quietly, "That was the bargain."

events.text: A young woman with a black heron stitched on her shoulder is waiting on the landing, very straight, very pale. "Maren Harrow," she says. "Of House Harrow of the Blackfen. My uncle Valen climbed here once, and came home with a knife and no gift, and never spoke of it. Before he died he told me what he did, and to whom." She kneels. "I came to make amends for my house."

choices.text: Accept her amends, and climb a floor with her

effects.log: You raise her to her feet. You climb one floor together. At the top she bows the eastern way, carefully, as if someone had taught her. "House Harrow owes you," she says. "We will not forget it this time."

choices.text: Tell her the debt was his, not hers

effects.log: She looks up, startled. "That is not how houses work on my side," she says. "Perhaps it should be." She goes down the stairs lighter than she came.

choices.text: Refuse: some things are not mended

effects.log: She stands and bows, and does not argue. "Then House Harrow will remember that too," she says, without anger, and goes.

events.text: A knight in white mail with a pale thorn branch painted on the shield stands on the landing as if he had been waiting for you. "Aldric Vey, Knight-Commander of the Order of the Pale Thorn," he says. "My order has heard of an eastern climber who will open the door between our worlds. We do not want it opened. I am sent to stop you." He does not draw. "Not today. Today I wanted to see your face. It is fairer to hunt someone you have seen."

choices.text: Let him look, and look back

effects.log: He studies you a long moment. "Ordinary," he says, almost disappointed. "They always are." He bows and goes up the stairs ahead of you.

choices.text: Ask him why his order fears the door

effects.log: "Because what comes through a door can go both ways," he says. "Armies. Gods. Plagues. Climbers." He looks at you. "You are not an army. I will report that."

choices.text: Tell him to try, then

effects.log: He nods, unoffended. "I will," he says. "Fairly. The Order hunts with its face shown." He goes.

events.text: Aldric Vey of the Pale Thorn comes down the stair at you with his sword drawn and his face bare, as he promised, and three knights of his order behind him. "Eastern climber," he says. "In the name of the Order. Yield, or fall."

choices.text: Beat them, and spare him at the last

effects.log: You beat all four, and hold your last blow a finger from his throat, and step back. He stares at the sword you did not use. "The Order did not tell me you would do that," he says.

choices.text: Drive them back down the stair

effects.log: You drive them back floor by floor until they turn and go. "This is not over," Aldric calls up the stairwell, and it is not: the Order of the Pale Thorn will remember the eastern climber.

choices.text: Lower your weapon and tell him what the door is for

effects.log: You tell him about the bell-caster and the stonewright and a question nobody answered. His knights look at him. He lowers his sword, slowly. "Then I was sent to stop a question," he says. "I will not." His knights follow him back down.

events.text: In the storm floors Aldric Vey of the Pale Thorn is on the stair again, alone, without his order's shield. "I left them," he says. "A knight you spare is a knight you keep. I climbed to see what the door is." Then the storm comes down on you both, and he steps in front of you with his bare sword raised, and the light takes him.

choices.text: Carry him to the next landing

effects.log: He is light in his white mail. "Fair," he says at the landing, "it was fair." Then he is gone, and the Tower rings one bell you did not ring.

choices.text: Take his pale thorn badge home to his order

effects.log: You take it from his shoulder. In some life, on the other side, someone of the Pale Thorn will see it and know what he chose.

events.text: A thin mage in black feathers waits on the landing with a book open in the air beside him. "Halden Crowe, of House Crowe, the mages of the Ninefold Stair," he says. "I have read every art of my sky. I want yours. I will pay, or I will take it. I would rather pay." The book turns a page by itself, toward you.

choices.text: Teach him a little, freely

effects.log: You teach him the first breath of your art, the one every child learns. He writes it down with shaking hands. "Free," he says. "Nobody gives anything free on the Ninefold Stair." He goes away troubled.

choices.text: Refuse him

effects.log: "Then I will take it," he says, regretful, "another floor." The book snaps shut. House Crowe has marked you.

choices.text: Ask what he would do with it

effects.log: "Know it," he says. "That is all a Crowe ever wants. Then the knowing wants more." He sounds tired of himself.

events.text: Halden Crowe springs his trap on the stair: a circle of black feathers that closes round you and begins, very politely, to read your art out of you like a book. "Forgive me," he says. "House Crowe does not take no." The feathers rise.

choices.text: Break the circle and drive him off

effects.log: You break it from the inside, feather by feather, and he flees up the stair with half a page of your art and none of its heart. House Crowe will hunt the rest of it, in other skies and other lives.

choices.text: Let him read one page, and offer it as a gift

effects.log: You stop fighting and let him read one page, and tell him it is a gift. The circle falls apart in his hands. "A gift cannot be taken," he whispers. "It ruins the rite." He laughs, and it sounds like the first true laugh of his life.

events.text: The tenth floor is one long room of old wood. An old porter in patched hemp is sweeping it with a willow broom taller than he is, a bamboo hat with a torn brim pushed back on his head. Sawdust turns in the light from the windows. He does not look up. "Floor ten has a guardian," he says. "The guardian is busy. The floor is dirty. There is a second broom by the door."

choices.text: Take the second broom and sweep beside him

effects.log: You sweep the length of the hall twice before he says a word. "Front heel," he says, and taps your ankle with the handle. When at last he lifts the willow broom like a spear, the fight feels like part of the sweeping.

choices.text: Tell him you came to fight, not to clean

effects.log: He sighs and sets his hat straight. "Everyone says that, the first time." The broom turns in his hands. He fights with nothing but the first form of every school there is, and never once a secret move.

choices.text: Bow to him as you would to a master

effects.log: He looks at your feet, not your face. "Clean," he says. "Nothing borrowed, nothing extra." Then he shows you, once, the plain form he has beaten ten thousand climbers with, and your own art sits steadier in you for it.

choices.text: Sit on the bottom step and rub your shins

effects.log: He sits down beside you with the broom across his knees. "You tried to win with the end of your art," he says. "I fight with the beginning of it. Come back when you remember the beginning." He brushes the dust off your sleeve before you go.

events.text: The porter is sweeping again when you reach the tenth floor, and this time he stops. He walks round you once, slowly, looking only at your feet. "I know these feet," he says. "Another life, another face. You still lean on the front heel." He taps the boards with the end of the broom. "One habit. Today I take one habit away from you."

choices.text: Let him correct your stance before the fight

effects.log: He moves your back foot the width of a finger. That is all. You fight the rest of the floor with a stance that feels strange and wrong and, by the end, like the one you should always have had.

choices.text: Show him the stance this life taught you instead

ok.log: He watches it for a long moment. "That one is new," he says. "Keep it. I will take a different habit." He does, the moment the fight begins, and you are grateful and sore in equal parts.

fail.log: He knocks it over with the broom handle before you have finished setting it. "Pretty," he says. "Pretty is the first thing to go." You fight the rest of the floor on his terms.

choices.text: Pick up the second broom without being asked

effects.log: He sees you reach for it and almost smiles. "You remember," he says. "Most people remember the fight. You remember the floor." You sweep together until the dust is gone, and only then does he lift the willow broom.

choices.text: Tell him that in this life you will sweep first

effects.log: "In the last one you would not," he says, and you have no memory of it at all. He hands you the second broom. "People change between lives. Not often. It is nice when they do."

events.text: This time the porter is sitting on the stair with his hat in his lap, the willow broom against the wall. He nods at the step beside him. "I was the first," he says. "The first one the Keeper let in. No root. Nobody would test me twice." He looks up the stairwell, into the dark where floor eleven waits. "I never went higher than this. Not once. Ask me why."

choices.text: Ask him why he stopped at ten

effects.log: "Because somebody had to be standing here," he says, "for the next one without a root. They come up those stairs thinking the Tower is like everything else. Then they meet an old porter who fights with the basics, and loses to the basics, and they understand."

choices.text: Ask him what the Keeper was like back then

effects.log: "Exactly the same," he says. "Same robe. Same cold tea. I think the Keeper was born old." He laughs, nearly. "No. The Keeper was born like you and me. That is the part nobody believes."

choices.text: Offer to take him up with you when you win

effects.log: He looks at you for a long time. "You beat me today," he says. "That is the only thing on this floor that gives anyone the right to offer. I will think about it. I have been thinking about it for a very long time."

choices.text: Tell him you understand, from the bottom of the stairs

effects.log: "You do not, yet," he says gently, and helps you up. "But you fell on the right side of it. Falling on the basics is no shame. Falling on pride is a long way down."

events.text: The porter meets you at the door with the willow broom held out across both palms, the way people hand over a sword. "I want to see floor eleven," he says. "Not climb it. See it. I do not have it in me to walk through that door. The broom does." He looks at the floor. "Carry it up for me. If you can get past me, that is."

choices.text: Carry the broom up the stair to floor eleven

effects.log: You climb with his broom over your shoulder, and lean it against the red lacquer of the next floor's door. When you look back down the stairwell he is at the bottom of it, hat in his hands, looking up at a door he chose never to open.

choices.text: Promise to carry it up next time

effects.log: He takes the broom back. "Next time," he agrees. "I have heard that before. I have heard it from people who kept their word, too." He sweeps the floor where you fell, slowly, saving the spot for later.

choices.text: Ask why he never carried it himself

effects.log: "Because if I go up those stairs," he says, "I will want the next ones. And then nobody is here for the ones without a root." He shrugs. "The broom can go. The broom has no ambitions."

choices.text: Refuse: a guardian's broom belongs to the guardian

effects.log: He nods slowly and takes it back. "Fair," he says. "Most things belong where they are." But you see him look at the stairwell once more before the fight, the way someone looks at a road home.

events.text: The porter is not on the floor when you arrive. He is standing at the top of the tenth floor's stair, at the very door of floor eleven, holding the willow broom. "Whatever happens today," he says, "I am walking you up." Afterwards he steps through the door beside you and sets the broom down on the red lacquer. It leans there a moment. Then it puts out a leaf.

choices.text: Laugh with him

effects.log: He laughs first, a cracked old laugh nobody in the Tower has heard in ten thousand years. You laugh too. By the time you stop, the broom has three green shoots and a root curling into a crack in the floor, and he is wiping his eyes with his hat.

choices.text: Kneel and press the root down into the crack

effects.log: You set the root firmly into the wood. "There," he says. "Now it lives here." He goes back down the stair without his broom for the first time in his long life. "I will know your feet," he calls back. "Every life. Lean on the back heel."

choices.text: Give him your own walking stick to sweep with

effects.log: He weighs it in both hands, frowning, then grins. "Too short," he says. "It will do." Whenever you climb the first floors from now on, in any life, someone has already swept them.

events.text: There is a willow sapling growing out of the floor of the eleventh landing, taller every life. The old porter meets you at the tenth floor with a stubby walking stick he uses as a broom. "Back heel," he says, before you have said hello. "Good. You remembered." You have met here {tw_chapter} times now, and he says it as if it were the first.

choices.text: Sweep the floor with him before you go up

effects.log: You sweep together without talking. At the door he hands you a willow leaf from the sapling. "For the stairs," he says. It does nothing at all, and you keep it.

choices.text: Ask him if he ever thinks of climbing now

effects.log: "Every day," he says. "Then the next one without a root comes up the stairs, and I think about them instead." He shoos you toward the door with the stick.

events.text: The porter catches you before you hit the bottom step and sets you down beside the sapling's roots as if you were a sack of rice. "Front heel," he says sadly. "You were doing so well." He has caught you here before, in other lives. He remembers every one.

choices.text: Ask him to show you the first form again

effects.log: He shows it, slowly, three times. It is the same form every child learns on the first morning. You watch it as if you had never seen it before.

choices.text: Thank him and go down to heal

effects.log: "Come back next year," he says. "The floor will be swept." It will. It always is.

events.text: The old porter of the tenth floor is sitting in a corner, nursing his wrist, his willow broom snapped in two. In the middle of the floor stands a knight in dented plate from another sky, a notched longsword in both hands and a lord's torn tabard over his armour. "Sir Garrick Thorne," he says. "I won this floor fair. If you want it, win it fair." His accent turns every word square at the corners. His tabard bears the stag of House Thorne of the Wealdmarch, a hedge-house of three farms and one old sword.

choices.text: Fight him straight, blade to blade

effects.log: He fights the way he talks: straight, heavy, honest. You meet him with the plainest forms you know, and somewhere in the middle of it he starts to grin, because nobody where he comes from moves the whole body behind a single cut.

choices.text: Find the gap between his armour plates

ok.log: His plate is good, but it was made for another sky's swords. You find the seam at the elbow where no western blade would go, and he swears in his own tongue, and laughs.

fail.log: You go for the seam and he turns, so the steel takes it. "Clever," he says. "My old lord liked clever. Clever did not save him."

choices.text: Help the old porter up before anything else

effects.log: The knight lowers his sword while you do it. "Fair," he says, surprised. The porter mutters that he is fine, and lets you help him anyway. Afterwards he sweeps the knight off his floor with half a broom.

choices.text: Take the hand he offers you off the floor

effects.log: He pulls you up in one heave. "You fight like water poured on a slope," he says. "I do not understand it yet. I will." He sits down by the porter, who glares at him, and waits for the next climber.

events.text: Sir Garrick holds the tenth floor again, in the same dented plate. He knows you at once. Before the fight he sits on the bench by the door and unbuckles a gauntlet. "My lord was hanged," he says, "for a thing I did. I stood in the crowd and let it happen. I climbed your tower to find a place where strength pays debts." He looks at his hand. "So far it only buys floors."

choices.text: Tell him strength never paid a debt it did not make

effects.log: He is quiet for a long time. "That is what my lord would have said," he says, and buckles the gauntlet on again. He fights you honestly, and slower, as if he were thinking about something else.

choices.text: Just listen until he has finished

effects.log: He tells it all: the crime, the trial, the rope. You say nothing. At the end he nods, as if you had answered, and stands. "Thank you. Now, if you please, the floor."

choices.text: Show him how to stand so the whole body is behind the blade

effects.log: He tries it, badly, then less badly. "Your masters teach this to children?" he asks. When you nod he shakes his head. "Where I come from we teach children to hold the sword up, and nothing else."

choices.text: Ask him to tell you how to stand, his way

effects.log: He shows you a western guard, high and stubborn, made for standing still while everything hits you. It is ugly and it works. You have never been so happy to learn something ugly.

events.text: The knight is not fighting anyone when you arrive. He is kneeling in front of the old porter, who is teaching him to sweep. Garrick looks up. "He says I cannot go home until I can stand like you do," the knight says. "I want to go home. I want to stand in front of my lord's grave and say it aloud." He gets to his feet. "One more fight first. A fair one."

choices.text: Fight him hard: he wants it fair, not easy

effects.log: You give him everything, and he takes it on the high western guard, and at the end he is breathing hard and smiling. "That," he says, "is what I needed to know I could survive."

choices.text: Tell him the confession matters more than the stance

effects.log: "I know," he says. "But a knight who cannot stand up straight cannot say it straight either." The porter, behind him, nods as if this were the wisest thing ever said on floor ten.

choices.text: Offer to walk him to the bottom of the stairs

effects.log: He looks surprised, then grateful. At the gate the Keeper is waiting with a cup of cold barley tea for him. "Your sky is different," the Keeper says. "Your feet are the same." Garrick bows to the Keeper the eastern way.

events.text: Garrick meets you at the door with his longsword sheathed and his tabard mended. "I said it," he says. "At the grave. Aloud. Nobody hanged me for it." He looks lighter by a full suit of plate. "I hold this floor today for the last time, I think. Beat me and I go home and train squires. Lose, and I stay and teach you to stand still."

choices.text: Beat him, and send him home

effects.log: You win it cleanly and he yields on one knee. "Clean," he says, which is what the porter says too. He gives the floor back to its guardian with a bow, and goes down the stairs to a door that opens on another sky.

choices.text: Lose, and learn to stand still

effects.log: He keeps his word. For an hour he teaches you to stand while he hits your guard, until your arms are numb and your feet are rooted. "There," he says. "Now nothing can push you off a floor you have earned."

choices.text: Ask him what he will teach the squires

effects.log: "Your stance," he says at once. "The eastern one, with the whole body behind it. I will tell them a hedge knight learned it in a tower from someone who would not give me their name." He grins. "Give it to me. I will tell them that too."

choices.text: Give him something of yours to take home

effects.log: You give him a plain cord from your sleeve. He ties it round the hilt of his notched sword. "When the squires ask," he says, "I will tell them it is from the east of the seam, and that the east does not forget a fair fight."

events.text: Sir Garrick holds the tenth floor again, in another life of yours, greyer, with two squires in mended tabards behind him. They bow to you the eastern way, both of them, badly. "Their stance," Garrick says proudly, "is yours. Mostly." He draws the old notched sword. "For old times. Fair."

choices.text: Fight him for old times, fair

effects.log: It is a good, honest fight, the kind you can only have with someone who has never once lied to you. His squires cheer for both of you.

choices.text: Correct the squires' feet before the fight

effects.log: You move their back feet the width of a finger. Garrick laughs until his armour rattles. "That," he says, "is exactly what the old porter did to me."

events.text: A young man with a lute on his back and ink on every finger is sitting outside the door of the tenth floor, scribbling. He jumps up when he sees you. "Pell Ashby, bard, from the other side of the sky," he says, all in one breath. "I am writing a ballad of every fight in this tower, and I am not brave enough to be in any of them. May I stand behind you? Not near. Just behind." The Ashby Players, he adds, a family of travelling bards eleven generations long, "all liars, all beloved".

choices.text: Let him stand behind you

effects.log: He stands behind you through the whole floor, shouting things like "Oh, well done!" and once "Duck!", which is not bad advice. When the old porter bows, Pell is writing so fast he tears the page.

choices.text: Tell him to watch from the door, where it is safe

effects.log: He watches from the door and narrates under his breath. When it is over he reads you the first verse. It is mostly lies, all of them flattering, and you are surprised by how much you like it.

choices.text: Ask him to write down the old porter's forms instead of the fight

effects.log: He frowns, then writes. "Front foot, back foot, the broom like this," he mutters. "It is not a ballad. It might be better than a ballad." He keeps the page.

events.text: Pell Ashby is waiting at the door of the tenth floor, older, his lute new, his grin the same. "You will not believe it," he says. "They sing it. Your fight. In inns on my side of the sky, they sing the song about the climber with no name who fought an old man with a broom." He hands you a folded verse. "I wrote you a new one. You have to win, or it does not scan."

choices.text: Read the verse aloud before the fight

effects.log: It is a terrible verse, and you read it aloud, and the old porter laughs, and Pell goes red to the ears. Then the porter lifts the broom, and Pell hides behind you exactly as he did the first time.

choices.text: Make him fight a little this time

effects.log: He holds his lute like a club and is very bad at it. But he stays on his feet, and he stays beside you, and afterwards he cannot stop telling you so.

choices.text: Win it so the verse scans

effects.log: You win, and it scans. Pell sings the last line from the top of the stairs, out of tune, at full voice, and the Tower's bells answer him with one of their own.

choices.text: Tell him to change the last line

effects.log: "To what?" he asks, writing anyway. "She fell? He fell? They fell, and got up?" He chews the pen. "They fell, and got up. Yes. That one is better."

events.text: Pell is waiting with no lute this time, only a plain staff and a face set like someone about to do something brave. "Teach me to breathe," he says. "The way you do, before a fight. I have sung about it in a hundred inns. I want to know what it is." Inside, the old porter is already sweeping, and listening.

choices.text: Teach him one breath, the first one

effects.log: You teach him the breath every beginner learns. He gets it on the ninth try. When the porter comes at you both, Pell holds the line beside you for three whole exchanges, breathing, and does not run.

choices.text: Teach him the deep breath you use before a hard fight

ok.log: You find a way to say it in his words. He breathes, and something in his face changes. He stands beside you through the whole floor, and at the end he is weeping and laughing at once.

fail.log: It is too much for him; he coughs and sits down. "Too soon," says the porter kindly. "Start with the first one." You do. He gets that one.

choices.text: Tell him the breath is not for songs

effects.log: He nods. "I know," he says. "That is why I want it." You teach him. Afterwards he does not write anything down at all, for the first time since you have known him.

events.text: There is someone at the door of the tenth floor humming a western ballad you have heard before: the climber with no name and the old man with the broom. It is Pell Ashby, grey at the temples now, breathing slowly and evenly the way you taught him in a life you barely remember. "You came back," he says. "The song said you would."

choices.text: Climb the floor together, like before

effects.log: He stands beside you, not behind. He is still very bad at fighting. He is very good at not running away.

choices.text: Ask him to sing the newest verse

effects.log: The newest verse is about a climber who keeps coming back, life after life, and a bard who keeps waiting at the door. It is the best thing he has ever written. He says so himself.

events.text: At an inn on the road, a travelling player sings a song in a tune nobody here knows: a climber, a broom, an old man who bows. The words are wrong in every place you know, and right in every place you do not.

choices.text: Pay for the singer's supper

effects.log: The singer eats and sings it again, slower. You know now who wrote it.

choices.text: Listen from the back and leave quietly

effects.log: You leave before the end. Some songs are better not heard to the last line.

events.text: The twentieth floor is a red lacquered hall of nine hundred hanging name tablets. A tall elder in layered crimson robes stands among them, red lacquer gauntlets on her hands, nine bone pins in her hair. She reaches up without looking and takes down one tablet. "The founder of the sect whose badge you wear," she says, reading it. "Let us see if you kept the art they left you, or only the name." She fights in that style, flawlessly.

choices.text: Answer the founder's art with the founder's art

effects.log: You fight the founder's forms with the founder's forms, and for a while it is like fighting a mirror. "Faithful," she says, and it is not quite praise. "But I asked whether it was yours."

choices.text: Answer it with what you added to it yourself

effects.log: You fight with the changes you made, the ones your teachers frowned at. She smiles behind the lacquer. "Ah," she says. "So the art grew. Founders like that, whatever their elders say."

choices.text: Bow to the tablet before you bow to her

effects.log: You bow to the founder's name first. She lowers the tablet and hangs it back gently. "Most climbers bow to me," she says. "The dead notice who bows to them."

choices.text: Ask her what the founder was really like

effects.log: "Impatient," she says at once. "Brilliant. Wrong about water." She helps you up off the lacquer. "They lost to me too. More than once. Come back."

events.text: The twentieth floor is a red lacquered hall of nine hundred hanging name tablets. A tall elder in layered crimson robes stands among them, red lacquer gauntlets on her hands, nine bone pins in her hair. "No sect," she says, reading you as if you were a tablet. "Then whose art is that?" She takes down the tablet of a master dead three thousand years, and fights in that master's style, flawlessly.

choices.text: Tell her the art is your own, stitched together

effects.log: You fight with everything you picked up on the road, from beggars and books and people who never meant to teach you. "Patchwork," she says. "Patchwork is still cloth." She seems pleased.

choices.text: Copy the dead master's style back at her

effects.log: You copy it well. She is better at it, because she has nine hundred more. "Copying me loses," she says. "Everyone learns that here. Some of them learn it twice."

choices.text: Ask her whose tablet will be next

effects.log: "Not yours," she says. "Not yet." She hangs the dead master back up and bows you toward the stairs. The red hall seems, for a moment, full of people nodding.

choices.text: Ask her how many tablets beat you

effects.log: "Today? One," she says. "In a hundred lives? Fewer every time." She helps you to the door.

events.text: Madam Hong-ryeon is waiting with a tablet already in her hand. It is blank. She turns it so you can see your name has not been cut into it, though the space is there. "I keep one for every climber who reaches me," she says. "Most stay blank. Yours I take out and look at sometimes." She hangs it among the masters, blank side out. "Too early to carve. Shall we see if it is too early to fight?"

choices.text: Ask what she would carve on it today

effects.log: "Today?" She considers you, head tilted. "Stubborn. Possibly kind. Leans on the front foot." She smiles. "That is not a line for the masters. That is a line for a friend."

choices.text: Tell her to leave it blank until you are done

effects.log: "Done?" she says. "Nobody is done. That is why the tablets hang, instead of lying in drawers." She draws a tablet from the wall, and fights you with a sword saint's art.

choices.text: Touch the blank tablet before you leave

effects.log: It is warm, the way wood is warm when someone has been holding it. She watches you do it and says nothing, and that is the kindest thing she has ever said.

choices.text: Ask her to show you which master beat you

effects.log: She shows you the tablet: a spear master you have never heard of. "Learn the name," she says. "That is the first thing an echo wants."

events.text: Madam Hong-ryeon is holding a tablet at arm's length today, as if it were hot. "This one is from your shelf," she says. "A person your soul killed, in a life you do not remember. They climbed to me once, after. They left an echo." She raises the lacquered hand. "I will fight as they fought. You may find you remember the end of it."

choices.text: Fight the echo and try to remember

effects.log: Halfway through the fight you know the next move before it comes, and the one after, and you know why. You do not remember the face. You remember the sound of the rain.

choices.text: Refuse to strike first at someone you already killed once

effects.log: She stops. The echo in her hands stops. For a moment the red hall is quiet. "That," she says, "is the first time anyone has refused." She fights you anyway, and gently.

choices.text: Ask her to tell them you are sorry

effects.log: She looks at the tablet. "They heard you," she says. "Echoes hear everything. That is the trouble with them." She hangs it up very carefully, a little lower than before.

events.text: Madam Hong-ryeon is sitting on the floor of the red hall, gauntlets off, her own tablet in her lap. You have never seen her sit. "I should tell you," she says. "I am an echo too. My living self climbed this far long ago, and left me here, and went down again. She is still alive somewhere. Old. Probably cross." She looks up. "Do you think she remembers me?"

choices.text: Tell her the living one surely does

effects.log: "Surely," she repeats, as if testing the weight of the word. "That is a climber's word. Very well." She puts her gauntlets back on, and fights you with her own art for the first time, not a dead master's.

choices.text: Promise to look for her living self

effects.log: She laughs, surprised. "In which life? There are a lot of old women with bad tempers." But she writes something on a slip of red paper and gives it to you: a name, and a mountain.

choices.text: Ask her what she would say to her living self

effects.log: "Keep climbing," she says. "You stopped at twenty. I would have liked to see thirty." She stands. "You will have to see it for both of us. Come."

events.text: Madam Hong-ryeon has a carving knife in her lacquered hand and your blank tablet on the table before her. "No fight first," she says. "This first. Then the fight." She cuts one line into the wood, slowly, in the old script. You cannot read it upside down. When she is done she blows the dust away and hangs it among the masters, between a spear saint and a poet.

choices.text: Ask her what the line says

effects.log: "It says what you are," she says. "Not what you did. What you did is on the other tablets." She will not say more, but every life after this the hall's lanterns lean your way when you come in.

choices.text: Bow to the tablet, as you would to a master

effects.log: You bow to your own name among the masters. The nine hundred tablets stir in a wind with no source. "They accepted you," she says, and she sounds prouder than you have ever heard her.

choices.text: Ask her to carve the next line next life

effects.log: "Only if you earn it," she says, and puts the knife in her sleeve. "You will. I am almost sure." It is the first thing she has ever been almost sure about.

events.text: Your tablet hangs among the masters of the red hall, one line cut into it in the old script. Madam Hong-ryeon touches it as you pass, the way a person touches a doorframe in their own house. You have met her here {tw_chapter} times. "Today I fight you with my own art," she says. "I save it for friends."

choices.text: Fight her own art with your own

effects.log: Two arts, nothing borrowed. It is the best fight you have had in years, and when it ends neither of you can quite say who won it.

choices.text: Ask her if her living self was ever found

effects.log: She is quiet. "An old woman on a mountain sent me a cup of cold tea," she says. "Through the Keeper. She said nothing else." She smiles. "It was enough."

events.text: There is a new tablet hanging in the red hall, above all nine hundred, in letters nobody here can read. Under it stands a lean man in a ruffled shirt with a long rapier and a parrying dagger, smiling a smile without a single scar near it. Madam Hong-ryeon sits by the wall, gauntlets folded, furious. "Cassius Vane," the man says. "The greatest blade of my sky. I hope to be the greatest of yours by dinner." The crossed blades of House Vane of Lucerra, the city of duelists, are embroidered on his cuff.

choices.text: Meet his rapier with the plainest sword form you know

effects.log: His blade is a needle and yours is a door. He dances; you stand. By the end he has stopped smiling and started paying attention, which is the best thing that can happen to a duelist.

choices.text: Match his footwork, step for step

ok.log: You match him step for step, and then take one he has never seen. He stumbles, catches himself, and laughs out loud. "Again! Show me again!"

fail.log: He is faster in a straight line than anything in your sky. He taps your shoulder with the flat of the rapier. "Point," he says. "And another, and another."

choices.text: Take his tablet down and give the hall back to her

effects.log: You take his tablet down and hand it to him. He looks at it, and at the furious elder, and bows to her with a flourish. "Madam. Your hall." She does not bow back. She does almost smile.

choices.text: Promise the angry elder you will be back

effects.log: Madam Hong-ryeon looks at you from the wall. "Bring a sword that does not bend," she says. Cassius, cleaning his blade, laughs. "That would be cheating."

events.text: Cassius Vane holds the red hall again, his tablet once more above the masters. He knows you before you are through the door. "You," he says, delighted. "The one who stands still on purpose. I have been practising standing still. It is the hardest thing I have ever done." He salutes with the rapier. "Teach me your footwork after, win or lose. I will pay you in mine."

choices.text: Agree: footwork for footwork

effects.log: After the fight you trade steps on the red lacquer for an hour. His are quick and narrow, made for a line; yours are wide and turning, made for a circle. Both of you go away with something the other's sky never had.

choices.text: Refuse: an art is not a coin

effects.log: He looks genuinely hurt, then thoughtful. "Where I come from everything is a coin," he says. "Perhaps that is why I climbed." He fights you without a single flourish, for once.

choices.text: Ask him why he wants to be the greatest

effects.log: "Because then," he says, "somebody would have to remember me." He says it lightly. It does not land lightly, and he knows it.

events.text: Cassius is not smiling when you arrive. He is standing under his own tablet, looking up at it. "I hung it there to be the greatest in two worlds," he says. "And every climber who beats me walks past it to the stairs and never looks up." He turns. "Madam Hong-ryeon says her tablets are looked at. By the dead. Every day." He lifts the rapier. "One fight. Then tell me how to be looked at."

choices.text: Tell him to take his tablet down himself

effects.log: After the fight he does it with his own hands, and stands holding it, a blade in a ruffled shirt with nothing above him. "Strange," he says. "I feel taller."

choices.text: Tell him to be a rival, not a monument

effects.log: "A rival," he repeats, testing it. "Someone who comes back. Someone who is remembered by one person, very well." He grins, scarless. "I like that much better."

choices.text: Look up at his tablet, for a long time

effects.log: You look up at it. He sees you do it, and for a moment the greatest blade of his sky cannot say anything at all.

events.text: The red hall is as it should be: nine hundred tablets, Madam Hong-ryeon among them, and Cassius Vane leaning on the doorframe with his rapier sheathed. His own tablet is under his arm. "I am giving the floor back," he says. "But not before one last fight. A rival's fight. Then I go home and come back in your next life, and the one after. Somebody has to keep you quick."

choices.text: Fight him as a rival, and send him home

effects.log: It is quick and bright and nobody is hurt. At the end he bows to you and then, very properly, to the elder. She bows back this time. He goes down the stairs whistling.

choices.text: Fight him and lose, and laugh about it

effects.log: He wins by a hair and refuses to gloat, which costs him visibly. "Next life," he says. "I will be slower. Possibly."

choices.text: Ask the elder to carve him a tablet of his own

effects.log: Madam Hong-ryeon looks at him for a long moment. Then she cuts a small tablet in the old script and hangs it at the very end of the row. Cassius stares at it and does not say anything clever for the rest of the day.

choices.text: Ask him what he will tell his own sky about this one

effects.log: "That the east has a hall where the dead are looked at every day," he says, "and that I was not the greatest blade in it. They will not believe me. I will enjoy that."

events.text: Cassius Vane is in the red hall again, in a new life of yours, with a little more grey and the same scarless smile. "My rival," he says, delighted, and salutes. His small tablet hangs at the end of the masters' row, and he touches it on his way past, the way the elder touches yours.

choices.text: Duel him, quick and bright

effects.log: He is faster than ever, and so are you. It ends in a draw neither of you will admit to.

choices.text: Teach him a step he has not seen

effects.log: He learns it in four tries and is insufferable about it for an hour. It is the best hour of the climb.

events.text: A stout friar in a brown cowl sits on the steps outside the red hall, his bare knuckles wrapped in knotted prayer cord, eating an apple. "Brother Odo Fairweather," he says, getting up. "From over the edge of the sky. I hear you lot fight with your fists and call it an art. I would very much like to see the eastern fist. From beside it, if I may." His cord is the knotted cord of the Friars of the Open Door, who never bar a gate to anyone.

choices.text: Let him fight beside you

effects.log: He laughs the whole way through the floor, even when the lacquered hand puts him on the ground. He gets up every time, still laughing, and swings like a church bell. By the end Madam Hong-ryeon is almost laughing too.

choices.text: Show him one form before you go in

effects.log: You show him the first form of the open palm. He copies it with enormous care and no grace at all. "Beautiful," he says. "Like a prayer with elbows."

choices.text: Tell him an art is not a show

effects.log: "Everything is a show to someone," he says cheerfully. "My god watches me fight. I like to give the old fellow something worth watching." He follows you in anyway.

events.text: Brother Odo has set out a meal on the steps of the red hall: bread, cheese, a small pot of something he swears is soup. "Eat first," he says. "Then the floor. Then you show me the eastern fist properly, and I show you the friar's fist, which is mostly forgiveness and an elbow."

choices.text: Trade forms with him over the meal

effects.log: You trade forms between mouthfuls. His are short and heavy, made for tavern doorways; yours are long and turning. By the end of the bread you both know something new.

choices.text: Ask him who taught him to fight

effects.log: "An abbot who used to be a soldier," he says. "He said a friar who cannot stand up for others is only a man in a brown dress." He laughs. "I have always liked the dress."

choices.text: Eat in silence, the way your teachers did before a fight

effects.log: He watches you, then does the same. When you go in together he is very calm, and fights better than you have ever seen him.

events.text: Brother Odo goes in ahead of you this time, rolling his shoulders, the prayer cord fresh on his knuckles. Halfway through the fight Madam Hong-ryeon draws the tablet of a palm master and strikes at you from your blind side. Odo steps in front of it. The blow sends him sliding across the lacquer on his back, and he lies there laughing.

choices.text: Help him up and thank him

effects.log: "Thank me? It was a fair sermon," he says, wheezing, "and I preached it with my ribs." He gets up. "Now, your eastern fist. Go on. I paid for a good seat."

choices.text: Finish the fight for both of you

effects.log: You finish it with everything you have. When it is done Odo is sitting up clapping, and Madam Hong-ryeon bows to him first, which nobody has ever seen her do for a stranger.

choices.text: Kneel by him until he can stand

effects.log: You stay with him until he can breathe. The elder waits, gauntlets lowered. "Your friend from the other sky," she says, "would have made a good tablet." Odo is delighted.

events.text: You hear Brother Odo before you see him: laughing on the steps of the red hall, older, rounder, his knuckles still wrapped in prayer cord. "There you are!" he says, as if it had been days and not lives. "I brought soup. It is worse than last time. Come on, the eastern fist and the friar's fist, together."

choices.text: Fight beside him again

effects.log: It is like no time has passed at all, except that he gets up more slowly, and laughs just as loud.

choices.text: Eat the terrible soup first

effects.log: It is terrible. You eat all of it. He watches you with enormous satisfaction.

events.text: The thirtieth floor is a hall of round bronze mirrors, each showing a different faint scene. In the middle stands a figure of polished bronze shaped exactly like you, its face blurred like breath on metal. When it speaks it uses the voice of someone you lost, and it says the thing you most regret, word for word, as if it had been there. Then it raises its hands in your own guard.

choices.text: Answer the voice before you fight

effects.log: You say the thing you never said, out loud, to bronze. The figure listens with its blurred face. When the fight comes it fights a little slower, as if part of it were still listening.

choices.text: Fight it and refuse to hear

effects.log: You fight your own techniques back at yourself, and win or lose, you do not listen. The voice keeps talking the whole time, softly. You will hear it on the stairs for days.

choices.text: Let the regret be heavy, and lift it anyway

effects.log: You do not answer it and you do not refuse it. You let it be what it is. The bronze face clears for a moment, almost into a face. Something in your chest goes quiet.

choices.text: Admit the voice was right

effects.log: You sit on the bronze floor and say it was right. The figure sits down too, exactly as you do. "Then we both know," it says, in your own voice now. "That is a beginning."

events.text: The thirtieth floor is a hall of round bronze mirrors, each showing a different faint scene. In the middle stands a figure of polished bronze shaped exactly like you, its face blurred like breath on metal. It searches you for a regret, and finds only small ones. "You travel light," it says, in your voice. "Or you have not looked." Then it raises its hands in your own guard.

choices.text: Tell it you have looked

effects.log: It studies you a long time. "Perhaps," it says. "Then I will fight you with what you are, instead of what you lost." It does, and that is harder.

choices.text: Ask it to show you a regret you have forgotten

effects.log: It shows you a small thing: a door you did not open for someone, years ago. You had forgotten it. You will not forget it again.

choices.text: Fight your own techniques without flinching

effects.log: Every move you know comes back at you. Power alone will not win this floor, but steadiness might.

events.text: The bronze figure is wearing a different face today. It is still you, but from another life: older, or younger, harder, a stranger you know from the inside. "Why did you leave that life the way you did?" it asks. "I was there at the end. I want to know." Around it the mirrors show a road, a room, a door closing.

choices.text: Tell it the truth, as far as you know it

effects.log: You tell it what you can. It is not much. The figure nods slowly. "That is all I knew either," it says. "It helps to hear it in someone else's mouth." Even if that mouth is yours.

choices.text: Tell it that life is over and this one is not

effects.log: It is quiet. "Fair," it says. "But the end of that one is part of the start of this one. Climb with it, not over it." It fights you as that old self fought.

choices.text: Ask it whether that life was happy

effects.log: "Sometimes," it says. "More than you think. Less than you hoped." The mirrors brighten for a moment on a summer afternoon nobody remembers but the Tower.

choices.text: Let your heart demon answer for you

effects.log: Something dark answers through your mouth, and the bronze figure takes it in like heat. "There," it says. "That is the part of you that has been answering for years." It fights you with it.

events.text: The bronze figure does not raise its hands today. It kneels in front of you on the bronze floor, its blurred face bowed. "I am made of every regret you carried up here," it says. "I did not choose to be. Forgive me for being you." The mirrors around it are dark for the first time.

choices.text: Forgive it

effects.log: You forgive it. It is harder than any fight in the Tower. The figure stays kneeling a long while, and when it stands its face is a little clearer, like a mirror wiped with a sleeve.

choices.text: Tell it there is nothing to forgive

effects.log: "There is," it says gently. "But you are kind to say so." It stands and fights you after all, and you have never been fought so carefully.

choices.text: Kneel down with it

effects.log: You kneel across from your bronze self. Neither of you says anything for a long time. When you both stand, the floor is cleared, though nobody threw a blow.

choices.text: Ask it to forgive you, too

effects.log: It looks up. "Yes," it says. Your heart demon, somewhere below thought, goes quiet for a whole season.

events.text: The mirrors of the thirtieth floor all show the same thing today: a small, stooped figure in a soot-grey hemp robe, much younger, reaching up from the ground toward a cloud. On the cloud a gifted child is being carried away. The bronze figure stands beside you, looking too. "Not your regret," it says. "The Keeper's. The Tower keeps the Keeper's as well. Nobody ever asks to see them."

choices.text: Ask who the child on the cloud is

effects.log: "A younger brother," says the bronze. "Taken up the easy way. The one below had no root, and was told so to their face." The mirrors go dark. You climb the next stair with a heavier step.

choices.text: Say nothing to the Keeper about it

effects.log: You keep it to yourself. Some things a person carries for ten thousand years are theirs to set down. The bronze figure nods, as if you had passed something.

choices.text: Carry a word of it down to the gate

effects.log: At the gate you only say, "I saw the cloud." The Keeper's broom stops for a breath. "It was blue," the Keeper says. "I still remember the colour." Then the sweeping goes on.

events.text: The bronze figure stands in the middle of the mirror hall with a crack running down its chest. "I have worn every face you gave me," it says. "I think I am done." The crack opens. Inside there is no person at all, only plain bronze bell-metal, dull and warm. It breaks a shard off itself and holds it out to you on its palm.

choices.text: Take the shard and keep it

effects.log: The shard is warm, like a bell that has just been rung. You will carry it in every life after this one, and some nights you will hear it, very faintly, from inside your own chest.

choices.text: Ask what the bell-metal is

effects.log: "Funeral bells," it says, "from a valley that is not there anymore. The whole Tower is cast from them." It closes your hand over the shard. "Now a piece of it goes with you."

choices.text: Thank it for every face

effects.log: You thank it, each face by name, the ones you remember. The bronze listens until you are done, and then it stands very still, and is only a statue, and the mirrors show only the room.

events.text: A bronze figure stands in the mirror hall with a crack down its chest, mended with a seam of brighter metal. It still has your shape, but its face is clear now, a plain face, not quite yours. "Old friend," it says. You have met here {tw_chapter} times. The shard in your chest hums when it speaks.

choices.text: Fight it as a friend

effects.log: It fights with your techniques and none of your regrets, which is a strange and clean thing to fight.

choices.text: Ask what the mirrors show now

effects.log: "Mostly you, climbing," it says. "It is a better show than the old one."

events.text: The bronze figure lies face down in a corner of the mirror hall. In its place stands a woman in a silver-grey gown sewn with shards of looking-glass, a hand mirror raised like a lantern. "Morwenna Glass," she says. "I came from the other sky to find a reflection that would never leave me." She turns the mirror. Out of the bronze mirrors step three copies of you, perfect, smiling. She is of the Glasswright bloodline of Merrowmere, whose mirrors are said to remember.

choices.text: Fight the copies one by one

effects.log: They are perfect copies, and so they make your mistakes. You learn more about yourself in that fight than in a year of meditation.

choices.text: Find the one copy that is not quite you

ok.log: One of them hesitates where you never would. You strike at it, and all three shatter into light. Morwenna lowers her mirror, impressed despite herself.

fail.log: They are all exactly you. That is the problem. You lose track of which one is real for a moment, and so do they.

choices.text: Ask her what she sees when she looks at you

effects.log: She looks for a long time, with her own eyes and not the mirror. "Somebody leaving," she says. "Everybody is, in the end." She lets the bronze guardian up off the floor without being asked.

choices.text: Tell her a reflection is not company

effects.log: "No," she says. "But it does not go away." Your copies bow and step back into the mirrors. She helps you up herself, which she did not have to do.

events.text: Morwenna Glass holds the mirror hall again. She is not fighting anyone. She is standing in front of the biggest bronze mirror, looking at herself. "I want to ask you something before the copies," she says without turning. "When you look at me, what do you see? Not in the mirror. In me."

choices.text: Tell her honestly

effects.log: You tell her: someone very clever and very tired, holding a mirror so nobody can see her face. She lowers it, slowly. She is younger than you thought. She does not raise it again for the whole fight.

choices.text: Tell her you see someone who climbed a long way

effects.log: "That is true," she says, "and kind, and not what I asked." But she smiles a little, and the copies she sends against you are slower.

choices.text: Turn her mirror toward the bronze guardian

effects.log: The mirror shows the bronze figure, face down, with its blurred face. Morwenna looks at it for a long time. "It is shaped like whoever comes," she says. "It has never had its own." She sounds as if she understands.

events.text: Morwenna has no copies waiting today. She has her hand mirror in her lap, face down. "I left home because everyone who loved me left me first," she says. "So I wanted a love made of glass, that would only ever do what I did. I have one now." She holds up the mirror. "It is the loneliest thing I have ever owned."

choices.text: Tell her to put it down and fight you as herself

effects.log: She does. Without the mirror she is quick and unsure and brave, and she fights better than any copy ever did.

choices.text: Offer to come back, in every life, as long as she holds the floor

effects.log: She looks at you as if nobody has ever offered to come back before. "You will forget," she says. "The Tower will not," you say. She has no answer to that.

choices.text: Ask the bronze guardian to speak to her

effects.log: The bronze figure gets up and stands in front of her and, for a moment, takes her shape. It speaks in her own voice: "Stay." She weeps, quietly, without the mirror.

events.text: Morwenna Glass is standing at the door of the mirror hall with a small bundle and no mirror in her hand. The bronze guardian is on its feet behind her. "I am going home," she says. "Before I go, one last fight, with no copies. And then I want to give you something."

choices.text: Fight her with no copies, and win

effects.log: She fights with nothing but herself and loses well. Then she gives you a little round mirror, no bigger than a coin. "It shows the truth," she says, "once. Do not waste it on yourself."

choices.text: Fight her, lose, and laugh

effects.log: She wins and does not know what to do with her face. Laughing is new to it. "I will send you something," she promises, "in some life, when you need it."

choices.text: Ask where she will go

effects.log: "Home," she says. "To people who might leave. That is the only kind there is." She kisses the bronze guardian on its blurred brow, of all things, and goes.

choices.text: Walk her down to the Keeper's gate

effects.log: The Keeper gives her cold tea and does not ask anything. "Your sky is different," the Keeper says. "Your feet are the same." She looks down at her own feet as if she had never seen them.

events.text: In another life of yours a small round mirror arrives at your door with no letter. When you look into it, it shows you one true thing, and then it is only glass. On the thirtieth floor, Morwenna Glass is waiting again, older, no mirror in her hand. "I hoped it was you," she says.

choices.text: Fight her, plainly, as friends

effects.log: No copies. No mirrors. Just two people on a bronze floor, and it is a good fight.

choices.text: Thank her for the mirror

effects.log: "Did it show you something useful?" she asks. You tell her it did. She is satisfied in a way she has never been satisfied by any reflection.

events.text: A pale woman with a scarf over her eyes waits at the door of the mirror hall, leaning on a staff hung with small brass bells. "Hesper Lowe," she says. "Oracle, of a sort, from the other sky. Mirrors cannot fool me. I cannot see them." She tilts her head at the sound of you. "You can. Shall we go in together? I will tell you where things really are." The Lowe seers of the Mistfen, she says, are all born blind, and all born listening.

choices.text: Go in together and follow her bells

effects.log: She walks in front of you, ringing the bells in a soft pattern. "Left. No, your other left. There." When you strike where she says, the mirrors cannot hide anything at all.

choices.text: Close your own eyes and fight by sound beside her

effects.log: You close your eyes. The hall is full of breath and footsteps and the ring of her bells. It is the first time the mirror floor has ever been fair.

choices.text: Ask her what an oracle sees

effects.log: "Not faces," she says. "Shapes. Yours is very stubborn." She laughs. "That is a compliment. Stubborn shapes reach the top of things."

events.text: Hesper Lowe waits at the door of the mirror hall with her staff of bells. After the floor, she sits on the bronze step and takes your hand in both of hers. "I can tell you one true thing about your next life," she says. "Only one. You may not like it. Do you want it?"

choices.text: Ask to hear it

effects.log: She says it in a low voice, close to your ear: one small true thing about a life you have not lived yet. You will forget it by morning. Some night in that other life, you will suddenly remember.

choices.text: Tell her to keep it for herself

effects.log: "Nobody has ever said that," she says. "Everyone wants to know." She squeezes your hand. "Then I will keep it, and be glad of it when it comes true."

choices.text: Ask her one true thing about her own life instead

effects.log: She is quiet. "I will go home and never come back," she says. "And I will remember this step for the rest of it." Her bells ring once, by themselves.

events.text: Hesper Lowe stands with you after the mirror hall, the bells on her staff quiet. "Everyone here has looked into a thousand mirrors," she says. "I have never once seen my own face. Will you tell me what it looks like?"

choices.text: Describe her face, slowly and truly

effects.log: You tell her everything: the line between her brows, the way her mouth turns up on one side, the small scar by her ear. She listens with her whole face. "Thank you," she says. "Now I know who has been doing all this."

choices.text: Tell her it looks kind

effects.log: "Is that all?" she asks. "That is the important part," you say. She laughs, and touches her own cheek as if checking.

choices.text: Take her hand and let her read your face first

effects.log: She reads your face with her fingertips, gently, then nods. "Fair," she says. "Now mine." You describe it. Neither of you will forget the other.

events.text: You hear the bells before you reach the thirtieth floor: soft, patterned, the way she rang them in a life you can barely remember. Hesper Lowe is waiting at the door, grey now, the scarf faded. "Your shape," she says. "Still stubborn. Good. Come, I will tell you where things really are."

choices.text: Climb the mirror floor with her again

effects.log: She guides you through the mirrors as if no time had passed. The reflections give up early.

choices.text: Describe her face again, as it is now

effects.log: You tell her about the grey, and the lines, and the scar by her ear that has not changed. "Good," she says. "I wanted to know how I turned out."

events.text: One evening, with no wind at all, a small brass bell hanging by your door rings by itself, in a soft pattern you have heard before: left, no, your other left, there.

choices.text: Go the way the bell says

effects.log: You walk where it tells you, and find a lost purse in the reeds, with a traveller's name stitched on it.

choices.text: Thank the empty air

effects.log: The bell rings once more and is still. Somewhere very far away, someone with a scarf over their eyes smiles.

events.text: The fortieth floor is iron: iron cage doors standing open, moss on the chains, great eyes in the dark. A broad, bearded warden in an iron-scale vest waits with a chain wound round one arm. Beside him stands Cheolgap, an ox-bear with an iron hide and moss on its horns. It lowers its huge head toward you, breathes in once, and sits down. It will not get up. The warden stares at it, then at you. "It smells a beast on you," he says. "A beast you were. It will not fight its own."

choices.text: Kneel and let it smell your hands

effects.log: Cheolgap breathes over your palms, slow as bellows, and makes a low sound you have not heard since a life with fur. The warden fights you alone, and gently, and with respect.

choices.text: Tell the warden you will fight him alone, then

effects.log: "Fair," he says, and unwinds the chain. Cheolgap watches from the floor the whole time, its eyes half closed, like an old relative at a wedding.

choices.text: Speak to it the way you once spoke, without words

effects.log: Something old in your throat remembers. Cheolgap answers. The warden lowers his chain and listens to the two of you, and for once he does not know what to say.

events.text: The fortieth floor is iron: iron cage doors standing open, moss on the chains, great eyes in the dark.
