A broad, bearded warden in an iron-scale vest waits with a chain wound round one arm. Beside him stands Cheolgap, an ox-bear with an iron hide and moss on its horns. "Tae-ak," the warden says, "and Cheolgap. I never strike first. It never strikes from behind. Begin when you like."

choices.text: Begin with a bow to both of them

effects.log: You bow to the man, and then to the beast. Cheolgap tilts its mossy head as if it had not been bowed to in a long while. The fight that follows is hard and fair.

choices.text: Go for the beast first, it is the bigger threat

effects.log: The warden's chain is between you and Cheolgap before you have taken two steps. "Wrong order," he says. The fight is very long after that.

choices.text: Wait for them to move

effects.log: You wait. They wait. It is the longest silence the iron floor has heard in years. In the end the warden laughs and steps forward first, against his own rule. "You win that one," he says.

choices.text: Get up from the iron floor slowly

effects.log: Cheolgap nudges you upright with the flat of one horn. The warden wipes your face with his sleeve. "Nerve," he says. "You have it. Now get the rest."

events.text: Warden Tae-ak is oiling the hinges of the cage doors when you come up, all of them open, all of them empty but for shadows that watch. "People think I keep them in," he says. "Every cage here is open. Has been since the Tower was built. The beasts stay because they choose to be climbed past. They like to see who comes." Cheolgap yawns hugely behind him.

choices.text: Ask why a beast would choose that

effects.log: "Because nobody else asks them anything," he says. "Out there, people hunt them or run from them. In here, people look them in the eye first." He nods at the dark. "They like being looked at."

choices.text: Look into the dark cages, one by one

effects.log: You look into every open cage before the fight. Eyes look back: tigers, cranes, a great carp in an iron pool. When you turn round, Cheolgap is standing, ready, and the warden is smiling.

choices.text: Ask the warden why he stays

effects.log: "Same reason," he says, and scratches Cheolgap behind the horn. "Somebody has to oil the doors." The beast leans into his hand like a dog.

events.text: Cheolgap is slower this time. Its iron hide is dull, and the moss on its horns has gone grey. The warden walks up to you with his chain hanging loose. "It is old," he says quietly. "It still wants to fight. It would be ashamed not to. Beat us if you can. But do not hurt it. Please."

choices.text: Win without landing a single blow on the beast

ok.log: You fight the warden through the beast's guard without ever touching it, turning its charges aside like water round a stone. At the end Cheolgap lies down, satisfied, and the warden puts a hand on your shoulder and says nothing at all.

fail.log: You try, and it is not enough: you touch its flank once, not hard. It does not mind. The warden does. "Nearly," he says. "Nearly is still kind."

choices.text: Fight the warden alone and leave the beast out of it

effects.log: You step round Cheolgap every time it comes, and fight only the man. It is harder than fighting both. Cheolgap seems to understand, and charges more slowly.

choices.text: Fight them both at full strength: it would want that

effects.log: You give it everything, and Cheolgap gives you everything back, one last time. The warden watches with his jaw set. When it is over the beast is panting and proud and, you hope, not hurt.

events.text: There is no beast beside the warden today. His chain is wrapped round both arms now, and his eyes are red. "Cheolgap died," he says. "Between your lives. In its sleep, in its own open cage, with the door open, the way it wanted." He raises the chain. "I fight alone today. I will fight badly. Do not let me win because of it."

choices.text: Fight him properly, as he asked

effects.log: You do not hold back, and he is grateful for it. He fights badly, as he said, and then in the last exchanges he fights very well, and at the end he sits down on the iron floor and weeps, and you sit beside him.

choices.text: Ask him to tell you about Cheolgap first

effects.log: He tells you: the day it walked in, the winter it slept on his feet, the climbers it liked. It takes a long time. When he is finished he does not want to fight anymore, and does anyway, gently.

choices.text: Leave something by the empty cage

effects.log: You leave a handful of the grass that grows by the Tower's gate in Cheolgap's cage. The warden sees it and turns away for a moment. "It liked that grass," he says hoarsely.

events.text: The warden meets you at the top of the stair with something small and stubborn pushing at his legs: a calf, iron-hided, with two bumps where its horns will be. "Cheolgap's line," he says. "Born in the old cage." The calf walks straight past him, straight to you, and pushes its nose into your outstretched hand. The warden laughs, the first time in two lives. "It chose," he says. "I did not teach it that."

choices.text: Let it follow you

effects.log: It follows you up the stairs, down the stairs, all the way to the gate, where the Keeper gives it barley tea. In every life after this, an iron-hided beast of Cheolgap's line will know your smell.

choices.text: Ask the warden to raise it for you, here

effects.log: "Here is good," he agrees. "It will be big. It will be stubborn. It will wait for you." He picks it up, with difficulty, and it does not stop looking at you.

choices.text: Name it

effects.log: You give it a name nobody else will ever use. The warden repeats it twice, carefully, so as not to forget. The calf seems to approve.

events.text: The calf is not a calf anymore. A young iron-hided ox-bear stands beside Warden Tae-ak, moss just starting on its horns, and when it smells you it bellows and nearly knocks the warden over. You have met here {tw_chapter} times. "It remembers," the warden says. "I told it you would come."

choices.text: Fight the two of them, gladly

effects.log: The young beast fights like its grandsire, all heart and no patience. You make sure it enjoys itself.

choices.text: Scratch it behind the horn before anything else

effects.log: It leans into your hand like a dog, the way the old one did with the warden. He watches with his arms folded and a look he would not admit to.

events.text: The fortieth floor is full of grey dire hounds, sitting in a ring, and over them circles a great storm-hawk of another sky, lightning in its wings. In the middle stands a man in a fur cloak and an antler helm, a horn on a strap at his hip. Cheolgap is chained to the wall of its own cage, and the warden beside it. "Brannoc Ironvale, of the Wild Hunt," the man says. "I came to cage the strongest beast of two worlds. Are you it?" The antlers on his helm are the badge of the Wild Hunt of Ironvale, oldest of the hunting lodges.

choices.text: Tell him you are not a beast, and fight him

effects.log: His hounds come in a grey wave, and the storm-hawk falls on you from above. You fight them without killing a single one. By the end Brannoc is watching that, more than he is watching the fight.

choices.text: Go straight for the man, past the hounds

effects.log: You go through the pack like wind through grass and reach him before the hawk does. He is strong, and old in the way of hunters. "Fast," he says. "Faster than my dogs."

choices.text: Unchain Cheolgap first

effects.log: The chain is iron from another sky, and it does not want to break. It does. Cheolgap stands up, and the warden stands up, and Brannoc lowers his horn and looks at you with something like envy.

choices.text: Watch how his hounds love him

effects.log: From the floor you watch the hounds come and lie against his legs, every one. Whatever he is, they love him. It is a strange thing to learn while losing.

events.text: Brannoc Ironvale holds the iron floor again, his hounds sprawled around him. Cheolgap is chained, calm, chewing. Brannoc is sitting on an overturned cage, sharpening a knife. "Your beasts do not fight to get out," he says. "Mine would. I do not understand this place." He points the knife at the open cages. "Explain it, and then we fight."

choices.text: Tell him the cages are open, and always were

effects.log: He gets up and walks round the floor, pushing doors. Every one swings. He comes back slowly and sits down again, and puts the knife away.

choices.text: Tell him beasts here come to be climbed past, not caught

effects.log: "Climbed past," he repeats, like a word in another tongue. "Not hunted." He looks at his hounds for a long time. "Mine came to me because I fed them."

choices.text: Ask his hounds' names

effects.log: He tells you every one. It takes a while. By the end of the list he is smiling, and the fight that follows is fierce and almost friendly.

events.text: The storm-hawk of another sky sits on Cheolgap's mossy horn today, and the old ox-bear does not seem to mind. Brannoc Ironvale stands looking at the two of them. "In my sky," he says, "the strongest beast is the one nobody can chain. I came to chain it. I think I came to the wrong place." He blows one short note on his horn. The hounds sit.

choices.text: Fight him for Cheolgap's chain

effects.log: You win the chain back in a hard fight, and he does not argue it. He unlocks it himself, at the end, and lets it fall.

choices.text: Ask him what he would do if he caught it

effects.log: "Show it," he says, "to the lords of the Hunt. And then, I suppose, sit with it." He sounds surprised by his own answer. "Like your warden does."

choices.text: Sit with the beasts and wait for him to decide

effects.log: You sit down by Cheolgap. After a while Brannoc sits down too, on the other side, and the hawk walks back and forth between you along the horn.

events.text: Brannoc Ironvale is standing at the stair with his hounds around him, the chain coiled over one shoulder. Cheolgap is free in its open cage. "I am going home," he says. "One more fight, for the Hunt's honour. Win it, and I let my hounds go when I get back. All of them. Lose it, and I will still think about it."

choices.text: Win it, and let him keep his word

effects.log: You win. He blows his horn once, long and low, and the hounds look up at him as if they know. "Free," he tells them in his own tongue. They do not leave his side, not one.

choices.text: Lose it, and tell him to free them anyway

effects.log: He helps you up. "Anyway," he says, rolling the word around. "That is the eastern part, is it? Anyway." He nods. "Anyway, then."

choices.text: Give the storm-hawk a feather of the Tower's own birds

effects.log: You find one under the eaves, grey and soft, and tuck it into the hawk's jesses. Brannoc looks at it and has to clear his throat twice.

choices.text: Ask him to send word how they choose

effects.log: "How they choose," he says, "yes." He laughs, a short bark. "You will hear. My sky is far, but my hounds are loud."

events.text: In another life a grey pup turns up at your gate with a leather collar stamped with antlers, and will not leave. On the fortieth floor, Brannoc Ironvale is waiting with three old hounds lying loose at his feet, no leashes. "You got the pup," he says. "Good. It chose you. They all choose, now."

choices.text: Fight him, with the hounds watching

effects.log: They watch and do not join in. Brannoc says that is how he knows they are free.

choices.text: Tell him the pup is well

effects.log: He wants every detail. You give him all of them. He listens like a father.

events.text: A woman in a green hood waits at the iron stair with a longbow on her back and a red-tailed hawk on her shoulder. "Elowen Brisk," she says, and nothing else for a while. Then: "Ranger. Other sky. There is a big beast in there. I can track its path for you. Which way it turns, which foot it favours." Her hood is the green of the Wardens of the Greenmarch, who guard a forest older than kings.

choices.text: Let her track it for you

effects.log: She reads the scratches on the iron like a book. "Left forefoot," she says. "Old. Turns right when tired." In the fight it turns right when tired, and you are ready.

choices.text: Ask her to track the warden instead

effects.log: She looks at you with real interest for the first time. "Smart," she says. "The man leads. The beast follows." She tells you where he will put his weight.

choices.text: Ask her why she climbs

effects.log: "Quiet," she says. "Everywhere else, people talk." Then she smiles, which seems to cost her something. "You do not talk much. Good."

events.text: Elowen Brisk has a small fire going on the landing below the iron floor, the smoke drawn up the stairwell. She nods at the other side of it. You sit. Her hawk looks at you, hops down from her shoulder, walks along your arm and goes to sleep there, head under its wing. Elowen stares. "It does not do that," she says.

choices.text: Keep still until it wakes

effects.log: You keep still a long time. She talks, a little, about forests where the trees are older than kings. When the hawk wakes you go up together and fight like two people who have known each other for years.

choices.text: Teach her a breath for waiting

effects.log: She learns it fast, the way hunters learn anything about stillness. "We have a word for that," she says. "It means: the deer has not seen you yet."

choices.text: Ask her the hawk's name

effects.log: She tells you. It is a word in her tongue that means something like "small thunder". The hawk opens one eye at its name and closes it again.

events.text: Halfway through the fortieth floor the warden throws his chain, and it wraps round Cheolgap's horns by mistake, and the old beast panics, thrashing, and the iron floor shakes. Elowen has an arrow on the string before you can turn. She looks at you, once, very fast.

choices.text: Nod at the chain, not the beast

effects.log: She shoots the chain. The arrow splits a link a hand's width from Cheolgap's eye, and the chain falls, and the beast stands trembling and free. The warden stops the fight to bow to her.

choices.text: Go in yourself and hold the beast still

effects.log: You get your arms round Cheolgap's neck and talk to it while Elowen picks the chain loose with her knife. When it is over all three of you are covered in moss.

choices.text: Trust her to choose

effects.log: She chooses the chain, of course. Afterwards she says, "You did not tell me. You trusted me." She says it as if nobody has, for a long time.

events.text: A red-tailed hawk is sitting on the rail of the iron stair. It hops onto your arm, settles, and puts its head under its wing. Further up, a woman in a faded green hood looks down. "It remembered first," Elowen Brisk says. "Then I did."

choices.text: Climb the iron floor with her again

effects.log: She tracks, you fight. Neither of you says much. It is perfect.

choices.text: Sit by a fire first, like before

effects.log: She lights it without asking. The hawk sleeps on your arm the whole time.

events.text: A red-tailed hawk lands on your windowsill one morning, with a strip of green cloth tied to its leg. It looks at you, unafraid, and waits.

choices.text: Feed it and let it go

effects.log: It eats from your hand and flies west, into the sky above the Tower, and is gone.

choices.text: Tie a strip of your own cloth beside the green one

effects.log: It lets you. It flies west with both. Somewhere a ranger will untie them and say nothing for a long time.

events.text: The fiftieth floor is green jade, every tile carved with the names of the dead. A judge in pale green court robes and a winged hat sits behind great jade scales, eyes bound with white silk. "Ok-pyeong," the judge says. "I do not fight with arts. Place your life on the scale." You do not know how, and then it is done. The scale tips. The heaviest thing you have done in this life steps down off the pan and turns to face you.

choices.text: Fight it, and own it as you fight

effects.log: You fight the thing you did, and you do not pretend it was anyone else's. The judge listens to the fight as if to testimony. "Owned," the judge says at the end. "That weighs less."

choices.text: Tell the judge it was justified

effects.log: "Perhaps," the judge says. "The scale does not ask whether. It asks whether you know what it weighed." The deed fights you harder after that.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the scale speak

effects.log: You let the scale speak. It speaks for a long time. At the end the judge nods. "Demonic is not a loss on this floor," the judge says. "Hypocrisy is. You were not a hypocrite."

choices.text: Bow to the scale before you leave

effects.log: You bow to it, not to the judge. Behind the white silk, something like approval. "The scale has been bowed to before," the judge says, "but not often by someone it just beat."

events.text: Judge Ok-pyeong has a ledger open beside the scales today, its pages very old. "Your soul," the judge says, "left something on the scale in a life you do not remember. I have the verdict here. Do you want to know what it was before it fights you, or after?" On the pan, something shifts in a shape you almost recognise.

choices.text: Before: you want to know what you are fighting

effects.log: The judge reads it out, flatly, the way clerks read. It is a small cruelty, a long time ago. You fight it knowing, and it is lighter for being known.

choices.text: After: you want to fight it first, blind

effects.log: You fight it blind, and only afterwards does the judge read it out. You had already guessed from the way it moved. "Most people do," says the judge.

choices.text: Ask whether the debt on your soul is this one

effects.log: The judge turns a page. "Part of it," the judge says. "A soul debt is many small things in a coat." The pan lightens by a hair as you look at it.

choices.text: Ask the judge to read it, and then to forgive it

effects.log: "I do not forgive," says the judge. "I weigh. Forgiving is for the person it was done to." A pause. "They did, as it happens. Long ago."

events.text: Today there is another life on the jade scales, not yours: a stranger's, from a hundred years ago, a merchant who saved a town and ruined a family to do it. Judge Ok-pyeong turns the blindfolded face toward you. "You judge," the judge says. "I will weigh your verdict." The scale waits.

choices.text: Judge the merchant guilty of the ruin

effects.log: You say it plainly. The scale weighs your verdict and finds it honest, if hard. "Hard is allowed," says the judge. "Cheap is not."

choices.text: Judge the merchant forgiven for the town

effects.log: You say the town outweighs the family. The scale tips slowly toward you, then away. "The family would not agree," says the judge, "but the scale is not the family."

choices.text: Weigh both, and refuse to give a simple verdict

ok.log: You give a verdict with two halves, and the scale balances, exactly, for the first time in years. The judge is silent a long moment. "That," the judge says, "is a judge's answer."

fail.log: You try to hold both, and it comes out muddled. The scale wobbles. "Close," says the judge. "Too close to nothing."

events.text: Judge Ok-pyeong is standing by the scales, the winged hat on the table, and one hand at the knot of the white silk. "You should see my eyes once," the judge says. The silk comes away. The eyes beneath are old, older than anything in the Tower but the Keeper, and tired. "I tested a nameless valley once," the judge says. "I took one child up on a cloud and told the other there was no road. I serve my penance here."

choices.text: Ask the judge whether the child below forgave it

effects.log: "I have not asked," says the judge. "The Keeper sweeps the gate below me every day. I have not asked in ten thousand years." The tired eyes close. "Weigh that."

choices.text: Tell the judge the penance looks just

effects.log: "It is," the judge says. "That is the worst of it. It is entirely just, and it does not end." The silk goes back on, gently.

choices.text: Tell the judge to go down and say it

effects.log: The judge looks at you a long time with unbound eyes. "Not yet," the judge says. "Not this floor." It is exactly what the Keeper says, and you wonder who learned it from whom.

events.text: The jade scales stand empty. Judge Ok-pyeong sits on one of the pans, blindfold off, hands folded. "Weigh me," the judge says. "The immortal who told a rootless child the road was closed. You climbed up the road I said did not exist. You are the one to do it." The other pan waits for your verdict. Far below, a broom stops.

choices.text: Forgive the judge

effects.log: You say it. The scale does not tip at all; it simply goes still, both pans level, like a held breath let out. The judge bows to you, very low. Far below, the broom starts again, and somehow it sounds lighter.

choices.text: Condemn the judge, and say why

effects.log: You say what was done, and to whom, and that it was wrong. The scale tips hard, and the judge does not flinch. "Thank you," the judge says. "Someone had to say it out loud, and mean it." The penance goes on, but it is no longer secret.

choices.text: Refuse: only the Keeper can weigh this

effects.log: The judge looks at you for a long time. "Yes," the judge says finally. "You are right. I was asking the wrong climber." That evening the judge goes down the stairs for the first time in ten thousand years, to the gate, carrying the scales.

events.text: The jade floor is quieter than it used to be. Judge Ok-pyeong still sits behind the scales, blindfolded again, but there is a cup of cold barley tea at the judge's elbow now. "From below," the judge says, when you look at it. "Every morning." You have met here {tw_chapter} times. "Place your life on the scale, climber."

choices.text: Place it, and fight what comes

effects.log: Whatever steps off the pan, you know it by now. You fight it as an old acquaintance.

choices.text: Ask about the tea

effects.log: "It is cold," says the judge. "It is always cold. That is how I know it is a real cup."

events.text: The fiftieth floor rings with steel. Judge Ok-pyeong sits bound with white silk at the wall, and the jade scales have been pushed aside. In their place stands a knight in white-and-gold plate behind a shield like a sunburst, a warhammer resting on her shoulder. She is perfectly calm. "Lady Seraphine Aldmoor," she says. "Inquisitor. My god went silent. I have come to find a law that still answers. I will judge you by mine." The sun on her shield is the sign of the Order of the Silent Sun, and the tower beneath it is House Aldmoor.

choices.text: Accept her judgement, and fight it

effects.log: Her hammer falls like a verdict, again and again. You meet it with everything you have. It is the hardest fight on the jade floor, and the least cruel.

choices.text: Ask her what her law says

effects.log: "That the wicked fall and the righteous stand," she says, "and that I can tell which is which." Her calm is very deep, and very thin.

choices.text: Spare her when she falls, and help her up

effects.log: She stares at the hand you offer. Force did not move her. This does. She takes it slowly, and on her feet she says, "In my law, that is not allowed." She does not sound sure.

choices.text: Ask her to free the judge, whatever she thinks of you

effects.log: She looks at the bound judge, then at you on the floor. "You ask for someone else, not for yourself," she says. She cuts the silk. "Noted."

events.text: Lady Seraphine holds the jade floor again. She has set the scales back up, carefully, and stands beside them as if guarding a shrine. "Your judge says these weigh deeds, not people," she says. "In my sky we weighed people. It was faster." She lifts the sunburst shield. "Tell me which law answers. Then we fight."

choices.text: Tell her a law that answers must also listen

effects.log: She is quiet a long while. "My god never listened," she says. "It only spoke. And then it stopped speaking." She fights you after that with no anger at all.

choices.text: Tell her no law answers; people do

effects.log: "Then I came a long way for nothing," she says, and then, slowly, "or I came a long way to meet one." She looks at you as if you were evidence.

choices.text: Ask her what her god last said

effects.log: "Strike," she says. "Only that. I struck. And then the silence." Her gauntlet tightens on the hammer. "I have wondered ever since if I heard it right."

events.text: Lady Seraphine has a case for you. "A starving thief stole bread from a starving family," she says. "In my law, the hand. In yours?" She waits, hammer down. The jade scales stand between you, empty. "Answer, and I will place your answer on them."

choices.text: Feed both, and punish no one

effects.log: The scale tips your way. She watches it as if it had betrayed her, and then as if it had saved her. "Both," she says. "Nobody in my order ever said both."

choices.text: The thief works off the bread for the family

effects.log: The scale settles, level. "Restitution," she says. "We had that word. We stopped using it." She writes something on the inside of her shield with chalk.

choices.text: Ask her what she would do now, not then

effects.log: She opens her mouth to say "the hand", and does not. Silence. "I do not know," she says at last, and it is the first honest thing her law has said in years.

events.text: Lady Seraphine meets you at the scales with her helm off. "One last fight," she says. "But I have learned your floor. It is not won by force." She raises the sunburst shield. "Show me mercy, if you can, while I try to beat you. If you can do both, I will believe there is a law that answers."

choices.text: Beat her, and spare her at the last blow

ok.log: You hold the last blow a finger from her helm and step back. She lowers the shield. "There," she says, very quietly. "That is the answer." She bows to the judge, and goes home to write her order a new law.

fail.log: You try to hold the blow and it is not quite enough; she staggers. But she saw you try. "Almost," she says. "Almost is the beginning of a law."

choices.text: Lower your weapon before she does

effects.log: You put it down first. She looks at it, at you, at her hammer. Then she puts hers down too. The scale beside you both tips, slowly, to level.

choices.text: Fight her hard, and let mercy be what comes after

effects.log: You fight her as hard as she deserves. Afterwards you help her up, and bind her cut, and that is the mercy, and she sees it. "Afterwards," she says. "Yes. That counts."

events.text: In another life a letter comes in a hand you do not know, sealed with a little chalk sun. It asks what you would do in a hard case: a sister who lied to save a brother. On the fiftieth floor, Lady Seraphine Aldmoor is waiting with the letter's twin in her gauntlet. "You did not answer yet," she says.

choices.text: Answer her, here, on the scales

effects.log: You answer. She writes it on her shield in chalk, beside a hundred other answers in a hundred hands.

choices.text: Fight her first, answer after

effects.log: She laughs, which she never used to do. "Very well. Force first, mercy after. I remember."

events.text: A man in a patched leather coat is crouched by the great jade scales of the fiftieth floor, a ring of lockpicks in his teeth. He grins round them. "Tobias Wick," he says. "Thief. Other sky. Those scales would buy a whole street where I come from. Help me lift them and I will fight your judge with you. Or stop me. Your choice." He grew up, he says, among the Lantern Row orphans of Saltquay, who are a family of a kind.

choices.text: Stop him: the scales belong here

effects.log: He puts the picks away, not very offended. "Thought you would," he says. "Had to ask." He fights beside you after all, mostly by tripping things.

choices.text: Pretend to help, then put them back

effects.log: You lift one end with him, then set it down exactly where it was. He looks at you a long time and then laughs. "That is a very eastern way of saying no."

choices.text: Ask him what he would buy with the street

effects.log: The grin slips for a moment. "Not a street," he says. "A roof. For some children who do not have one." Then it comes back. "Never mind. Let us fight your judge."

events.text: Tobias Wick is sitting on the jade stair with his lockpicks in his lap and no grin at all. "I should tell you why I steal," he says. "There is an orphanage in my city. Thirty children. A roof that leaks. Nobody pays for it but me." He looks up at the scales. "Every coin I ever took went into that roof. Does your judge weigh that?"

choices.text: Tell him the judge weighs everything

effects.log: "Then I am in trouble either way," he says, and laughs, and wipes his eyes. He fights the judge's deeds beside you like a man defending a roof.

choices.text: Give him a spirit stone for the roof

effects.log: He looks at the purse in his hand as if it might bite him. "Nobody has ever given me anything," he says. "I do not know how to hold it." He holds it very carefully.

choices.text: Ask him the children's names

effects.log: He knows every one, and their ages, and who is afraid of thunder. By the end you could find that orphanage blind.

events.text: Halfway through the fiftieth floor the scale tips hard against you: some deed of yours, heavy as iron. Tobias Wick looks at it, at you, and steps up onto the other pan before anyone can stop him. "Put mine on," he tells the judge. "The roof. The thirty. All the locks I picked for them." The pan sinks under him.

choices.text: Let him, and thank him

effects.log: The scale levels. The judge is silent for a long moment. "That is allowed," the judge says at last, "and very rare." Tobias steps down shaking and grinning. "Worth it," he says.

choices.text: Tell him to step down: your deed is yours

effects.log: He refuses. "Too late. I am already on it." The judge weighs you both together, and the floor is cleared or lost, but not by you alone.

choices.text: Step onto the pan beside him

effects.log: You stand on the pan with him, both your deeds together. The scale does not know what to do. The judge laughs, once, which nobody has heard in ten thousand years.

events.text: Someone has picked the lock of a door that has no lock, on the jade stair. Tobias Wick is sitting behind it, greyer, with a ring of new picks. "The roof is fixed," he says before you can ask. "Slates. Real ones. The thirty are fifty now. Some of them are thieves." He winks. "Honest ones."

choices.text: Climb the floor with him

effects.log: He trips the judge's deeds as cheerfully as ever. The scale seems almost fond of him now.

choices.text: Ask about the children

effects.log: He tells you every name. It takes until the bell.

events.text: The sixtieth floor is a silver archive of scrolls rising into darkness, each scroll a life. A tall figure in silver mourning robes and a silver veil walks the shelves with a lantern of many small flames. "Baek-ui," it says. Its voice is neither old nor young. It pulls one scroll from your shelf without looking. "Your most famous life. Let us see if you are more than it." It opens the scroll, and becomes it, and attacks.

choices.text: Fight your famous life with this life's arts

effects.log: It knows everything you knew then, and nothing you know now. You win or lose in the gap between. "More," the Archivist says afterwards, rolling the scroll shut. "Or different. I have not decided which."

choices.text: Fight it with its own techniques, better

effects.log: You do what it did, but sharper. The Archivist reads you a line from the scroll as it falls: something you said, then, that you do not remember saying. It was not kind.

choices.text: Fight the throne you once sat on

effects.log: The scroll it opened has a crown in it. The past life fights like someone used to being obeyed. You do not obey.

choices.text: Fight the god you were to a small world

effects.log: It opens a scroll that smells of rain on a world you made. Your old divinity fights you, puzzled that you would stand against it.

events.text: The Archivist holds a different scroll today, at arm's length, as if it were heavier than the others. "The life you are most ashamed of," it says. "I will fight as it fought. You may stop me at any time by saying why." The lantern's flames lean away from the scroll.

choices.text: Say why, before the first blow

effects.log: You say it. It takes a long time and nobody interrupts. When you are done the Archivist rolls the scroll shut without opening it. "Then I do not need to," it says, and fights you as yourself.

choices.text: Fight it to the end without a word

effects.log: You fight your shame to the end. It knows every excuse you ever made, and uses them. Afterwards, on the silver floor, you say why anyway, to nobody.

choices.text: Ask the Archivist which life it is

effects.log: "You know," says the Archivist, and you do. The flames of the lantern go still. "Most people think it is a different one. Most people are wrong about their own shame."

choices.text: Let your heart demon read the scroll aloud

effects.log: It reads with relish. Every word is true. The Archivist lets it finish, then closes the scroll on its voice like a lid.

events.text: The Archivist leads you past your own shelf, deeper into the dark, to a single scroll on a high ledge. "Older than your first remembered life," it says. "Yours. Written in a hand I do not know." It unrolls an inch. The writing is not any script you have seen, and yet you can almost read it.

choices.text: Try to read it

effects.log: You make out one word, and you are sure of it, and by the time you reach the stairs it is gone. The Archivist writes something in its own ledger: the date, your face, the word you forgot.

choices.text: Ask the Archivist who wrote it

effects.log: "I do not know," it says. "That is why I keep it on the high shelf. The only scroll in this archive I cannot read." It sounds, for once, almost afraid.

choices.text: Leave it rolled up

effects.log: You leave it. Some lives are not yours to read yet. The Archivist puts it back with great care, and fights you after with your own most ordinary life, a farmer's, which is somehow hardest.

events.text: The Archivist shows you a shelf at the very end of the archive, with one scroll on it. It is very old, and only a few lines long, and then it stops, mid-word. "The Keeper's," it says. "One life. The rest were given away so the Tower could remember the rest of you." The lantern's flames bow toward it, all together.

choices.text: Read the lines that are there

effects.log: A bell-caster. A valley. A younger sibling with a root. A cloud. Then nothing. You read it twice, and the second time you notice the last word is not finished, as if the writer were called away.

choices.text: Ask if the scroll can ever go on

effects.log: "If the Keeper is ever born again," the Archivist says. "There is space." It touches the empty silk below the last line, very gently. "I keep it dusted."

choices.text: Bow to the shelf

effects.log: You bow. The Archivist bows beside you, veil to the floor. Of all the shelves in the archive, it is the only one the Archivist bows to.

events.text: The Archivist meets you at the silver door with a scroll in its silver hand: blank, freshly cut, the rollers new. Beside it, on the shelf, the Keeper's single unfinished scroll. "This one is for the life after the Tower," it says. "Whatever you do when there is no more climbing. I will not shelve it. You will carry it."

choices.text: Take the blank scroll

effects.log: It weighs nothing. It will weigh nothing in every life after this. But some nights you will feel it in your sleeve, and think about what goes on it.

choices.text: Ask what you should write on it

effects.log: "Nothing," says the Archivist. "You do not write a life. You live it, and it writes itself. I only shelve them." It closes your fingers round the rollers.

choices.text: Ask it to keep the Keeper's scroll beside yours

effects.log: The Archivist is quiet. Then it moves the Keeper's unfinished scroll to the shelf beside your name. "Company," it says. "Both of you could use some."

events.text: The Archivist is reading when you arrive, a scroll from your shelf, and it reads you a line from it without looking up: something you did as a child, in a life you have forgotten, that was kind. You have met here {tw_chapter} times. "Still more than your past," it says. "Shall we test it again?"

choices.text: Fight whatever life it opens

effects.log: It opens a scroll at random. You fight yourself from somewhere long ago, and are gentle with them.

choices.text: Ask it to read another line

effects.log: It reads you three. They are all small. All of them are good.

events.text: The silver archive is ticking. A man in a dark blue scholar's coat stands among the shelves with an hourglass for a staff, clocks ticking in his sleeves. The Archivist sits on the floor with its lantern out. "Corvin Ashgrave," the man says politely. "Chronomancer. I came here to undo one death. I will undo anyone who stands in the way." When you strike, the sand in his staff runs backward, and so does your blow. His coat bears the hourglass of House Ashgrave, keepers of the Hourward for nine generations.

choices.text: Keep striking, faster than he can turn the glass

effects.log: He rewinds you once, twice, ten times. On the eleventh he is too tired to turn it. "Persistent," he says, breathing hard. "That is a kind of time too."

choices.text: Strike at the hourglass, not the man

ok.log: You strike the moment between the sand falling and the sand rising. The glass stalls. Corvin looks at it with horror, then with something like admiration.

fail.log: He sees it coming and turns the glass. You are back where you started, and so is the blow.

choices.text: Ask whose death he wants to undo

effects.log: "My sister's," he says. "A fall. A stair. One minute. I only need one minute." He relights the Archivist's lantern before he leaves, which you did not expect.

choices.text: Ask him if he has undone his own mistakes

effects.log: He laughs without much in it. "Every one," he says. "That is why I make so many." He winds back the ache in your shoulder, just a little, before you go.

events.text: Corvin Ashgrave holds the silver floor, and the Archivist stands by its shelves, lantern lit, watching him with its veiled face. "It has her scroll," Corvin says to you, low. "My sister's. Every life is here. If I take hers and turn the glass, she never falls." His hand is on the hourglass. "Fight me, and tell me why I should not."

choices.text: Tell him she would have to live that minute again

effects.log: "And every minute after," you say. He goes still. "I had not thought," he says, "what it would be like for her." He fights you, after, slowly.

choices.text: Ask the Archivist to show him her scroll, unopened

effects.log: It does. It is a short scroll, and a happy one, all the way to the stair. Corvin looks at it for a long time without touching it.

choices.text: Tell him you would do the same

effects.log: He looks at you, surprised. "Would you?" "Yes," you say. "And I would be wrong." He laughs, and it hurts him. "That is the problem. So would I."

events.text: The clocks in Corvin's sleeves have stopped. He is sitting on the silver floor with the hourglass across his knees and his sister's scroll in his lap, still rolled. "I could do it now," he says. "One turn. You could not stop me." He looks at you. "Fight me anyway. I want somebody to try."

choices.text: Fight him, and try to stop the turn

effects.log: You fight him all the way across the archive. At the last moment his hand is on the glass, and he does not turn it. You did not stop him. He stopped.

choices.text: Sit down beside him instead

effects.log: You sit. Neither of you says anything. After a long time he hands the scroll back to the Archivist, still rolled, and puts his face in his hands.

choices.text: Ask him what she was like

effects.log: He tells you. It takes the rest of the day. At the end the scroll is still closed, and he is still sitting there, but he is smiling.

events.text: Corvin Ashgrave is waiting at the silver door with his hourglass staff broken across his knee, sand in a little heap on the floor. "I chose not to rewind," he says. "It was the hardest thing I have ever done. Fight me one last time with no time tricks, and then I will go home and live in the right order."

choices.text: Fight him in the right order

effects.log: Blow after blow, and none of them taken back. It is a clumsy, honest fight, and when it is over he bows to the Archivist and goes down the stair at an ordinary pace.

choices.text: Give him something to measure time the slow way

effects.log: You give him a stick of incense. "It burns once," you say. "Then it is gone." He holds it as if it were the most precious thing in the archive.

choices.text: Ask the Archivist to shelve his sister's scroll beside his

effects.log: The Archivist does it without a word. Corvin watches the two scrolls side by side and nods, once, and leaves.

events.text: In another life a small package arrives: a silver pocket watch, stopped at one minute past an hour. There is no note. On the sixtieth floor, Corvin Ashgrave is waiting in a coat with no clocks in its sleeves. "Did it come?" he asks. "I stopped it the minute I decided not to. I wanted someone to have it."

choices.text: Fight him, in the right order

effects.log: No time tricks. He is slower than he was, and happier.

choices.text: Tell him you keep it on your desk

effects.log: "Good," he says. "Never wind it." You never will.

events.text: A young woman in a plain grey habit sits on the silver stair, a wooden holy sign round her neck, looking at the scrolls above her as if they might fall. "Mira Thistledown," she says. "Cleric. I think. I do not remember anything before the Tower's gate on my side." She swallows. "The Archivist has my scroll. I am afraid to read it. Will you go in with me?" Her holy sign is carved with the thistle of the Grey Sisters of Thistledown Abbey.

choices.text: Go in with her

effects.log: She holds your sleeve the whole way through the floor, and blesses you each time you are hit, in a language you do not know. It helps more than it should.

choices.text: Tell her she does not have to read it

effects.log: "I know," she says. "That is why I am frightened. If I do not have to, I might not, and then I will never know." She stands. "Let us fight first."

choices.text: Ask her what she does remember

effects.log: "Kindness," she says. "I remember being kind to people, but not who." She smiles. "It is not a bad thing to have left."

events.text: After the sixtieth floor, the Archivist holds out a scroll to Mira Thistledown: hers. Her hands shake. "Will you read it with me?" she asks you. "Not for me. With me." The silver hall is very quiet.

choices.text: Read it with her, line by line

effects.log: It is a long life for someone so young: a village, a fever, a promise made to someone dying. She cries at the promise, and then laughs, because she kept it. "I kept it," she says. "I kept it."

choices.text: Read it to her, so she can listen

effects.log: You read it aloud, slowly. She sits with her eyes closed and her hands in her lap. At the end she opens them, and she knows who she is, and is not sure she wants to be.

choices.text: Let her read it alone, and wait at the door

effects.log: You wait. It takes a long time. When she comes out she is very calm, and walks beside you to the stairs without a word, and squeezes your hand once at the bottom.

events.text: Mira Thistledown meets you at the silver door with her scroll under her arm and her holy sign in her hand. "I know who I was," she says. "Now I have to choose who I am. I think I choose this: someone who blesses the next life of the people she climbs with." She raises the sign. "May I?"

choices.text: Bow your head for the blessing

effects.log: She blesses your next life in her own tongue, slowly, word by word. It does nothing you can see. In your next life, sometimes, strangers will be kind to you for no reason.

choices.text: Bless her next life in return, your way

effects.log: You do it the only way you know, a bow and a wish. She laughs and cries at once. "Nobody has ever blessed a cleric," she says.

choices.text: Ask her who she chooses to be

effects.log: "Mira," she says. "That part I keep. The rest I am making up as I go." She grins. "Like everyone, I think."

events.text: There is a woman in a grey habit on the silver stair, older now, a wooden holy sign worn smooth round her neck. "I blessed this life of yours," Mira Thistledown says, "a long time ago. Has it been kind?" She stands. "Come. The Archivist has your shelf open."

choices.text: Climb the silver floor with her again

effects.log: She blesses every blow you take. It still helps more than it should.

choices.text: Tell her strangers have been kind

effects.log: She is so pleased she forgets to be solemn for the rest of the floor.

events.text: The seventieth floor is one immense array of gold lines that shift like water. In the middle of it a round, cheerful grandmaster in gold-thread robes sits on a cushion with a giant gold abacus on his back. "Geum-ha," he says. "Sit, sit. Do you drink green tea or the roasted kind? I never move, you see. The array does the fighting." He flicks one bead. The whole floor turns a quarter circle under you.

choices.text: Answer his tea question first

effects.log: "Roasted," you say, and he beams. "A person of sense." He chats about tea the whole time the array tries to fold you in half, and you solve it between sips of a conversation.

choices.text: Ignore the chat and read the array

ok.log: You find the pattern under the pattern: every bead he moves turns the room, but only clockwise. You step the other way. He claps his hands. "Oh, very good. Very good. I shall have to try."

fail.log: The lines shift faster than you can read them. You end up where you started three times. "It does that," he says sympathetically, pouring.

choices.text: Smash the array lines with raw force

effects.log: Every blow you land makes the gold lines brighter and the array stronger. He winces, kindly. "Brute force feeds it," he says. "Everybody tries once."

choices.text: Ask to keep the score of what you solved

effects.log: "Of course! I keep everyone's." He produces a little gold-edged book. "One solved, today. And, ah, how many unsolved?" He writes, chuckling.

events.text: Geum-ha has drawn a new array today, and it has two centres. "Two hands," he says happily. "It can only be solved by two people at once, one in each heart. I do so love company." He looks round the empty gold floor. "Did you bring anyone?"

choices.text: Ask the grandmaster himself to take the other centre

effects.log: He laughs until the abacus rattles. "Nobody has ever asked the array to solve itself!" He sits in the other centre. Together you turn the lines like a door.

choices.text: Wait for the climber racing you to come up

effects.log: You wait on the gold until your rival climbs into view, suspicious. You explain. For one floor, the two of you work as one pair of hands.

choices.text: Try to hold both centres alone

effects.log: You stand with one foot in each heart and turn both with your qi, badly. Geum-ha watches with deep interest. "That should not work," he says. "It is not working, but it should not even be not working."

events.text: Geum-ha is not smiling today. He has stopped the array halfway through a turn, and he points with a bead at a part of the gold floor near the wall. "Look there," he says. "Those are not characters. I have looked at them for a very long time. They are letters, from a script no scholar here can read."

choices.text: Study the letters

effects.log: They are straight where characters curve, and they sit in a line like fence posts. You copy three of them into your sleeve. They mean nothing to you yet. They will.

choices.text: Ask him who drew them

effects.log: "I do not know," he says. "I came here to master this floor and found half of it already drawn by someone else." He frowns at the abacus, which is not like him.

choices.text: Solve the array around the letters, leaving them alone

effects.log: You work round them like a stream round stones. He watches, nodding slowly. "Respect for what you do not understand," he says. "Rarer than talent."

events.text: Geum-ha pours two cups of tea before anything else today, which he has never done. "I should confess," he says. "I have never fully understood my own floor. Half of the array was drawn by the foreign mason, the one the Keeper calls a friend. I solve my half. The other half I only pretend." He looks at his abacus. "Every climber thinks the Golden Abacus knows everything."

choices.text: Tell him you will learn the other half with him

effects.log: He sets the cup down very carefully. "With me," he says. "Not instead of me." He wipes his eyes on a gold sleeve. "Yes. Yes, I would like that."

choices.text: Ask who the foreign mason was

effects.log: "Someone who laid stones without asking permission," he says. "That is all the Keeper ever says. I think the Keeper misses them very much."

choices.text: Tell him pretending kept the floor standing

effects.log: He laughs, a little wet. "That is the kindest thing anyone has said about my lies." He flicks a bead, and the array fights you as hard as ever.

events.text: The array of the seventieth floor is still. Geum-ha sits in his half of it, and you sit in the other, the half drawn in letters. "Together," he says. You move the lines; he moves the beads. Slowly the gold forms a word neither of you can read. Then, from the far side of the floor, a little brass voice in your memory reads it for you, and you know it: a name. Tamsin.

choices.text: Say the name aloud

effects.log: You say it. Every gold line on the floor glows at once, and far below, at the gate, somebody drops a broom. Geum-ha whispers the name back, testing it. "The mason," he says. "At last."

choices.text: Write the name in his score book

effects.log: He hands you the gold-edged book and you write it on the first page. "There," he says. "Solved. Both halves." He closes the book and holds it to his chest.

choices.text: Take the name down to the Keeper

effects.log: At the gate you only say it, once. The Keeper is quiet a long time. "Yes," they say. "Tamsin laid the stones. I poured the bronze." They pour you a cup of tea. It is, for once, warm.

events.text: Geum-ha has the gold-edged score book open when you arrive, with the mason's name on its first page. "Tea?" he asks. You have met here {tw_chapter} times. "I am keeping score. You are winning, mostly. Not the time in the third life with the spiral. We do not talk about the spiral."

choices.text: Solve today's array with him

effects.log: Both halves, together. He hums the whole time.

choices.text: Ask about the spiral

effects.log: "We do not talk about the spiral," he says firmly, and then tells you all of it.

events.text: The gold floor is covered with rune circles that orbit in the air like little moons. Geum-ha sits tied to his own abacus. In the middle stands a man in long violet robes with a crystal-tipped staff. "Archmage Theron Kell," he says. "I climbed to prove that your arrays and my circles are one science. Your grandmaster disagreed. Loudly." His circles close round you like a cage of light. He wears the violet of the Kell Collegium, the tower of mages that taught half his sky.

choices.text: Read his circle like an array

ok.log: It is an array: a strange one, written in rings instead of squares, but an array. You find its anchor rune and step on it. Theron stares. "You read it. You read my circle with your eyes."

fail.log: You read it as an array and it is not quite one. The rings close. "Nearly," Theron says. "Nearly is my whole thesis."

choices.text: Break the circles with force

effects.log: The circles shatter, but each shard becomes a smaller circle. Theron nods. "Force feeds it. Your grandmaster said the same of his array. You see? One science."

choices.text: Untie Geum-ha and solve it together

effects.log: Geum-ha takes one look at the circles and gasps with delight. "Oh, it is round!" Together you turn Theron's cage into a door, and the archmage is too interested to be angry.

choices.text: Ask him what he has learned so far

effects.log: "That your grandmaster is very stubborn," Theron says, "and very right about tea." He helps you up with a little spell that feels like a hand.

events.text: Theron Kell holds the gold floor again, but today he and Geum-ha are arguing on the same side of a table. Rune circles and bead-lines are scribbled all over it. "We need a third view," Theron says to you. "A climber's. Fight me, and then tell us which of us is wrong."

choices.text: Tell them both are right, in different shapes

effects.log: They look at each other. Geum-ha laughs first. Theron, reluctantly, second. "A square circle," he mutters. "Heresy. Write it down."

choices.text: Offer to trade him a page of arrays for a page of runes

effects.log: You write out the simplest array you know. He writes out the simplest circle. You both go away frowning at a page, which is how scholars are happy.

choices.text: Fight him and say nothing

effects.log: He fights with circles; you answer with what the grandmaster taught you. Afterwards he writes notes on his sleeve for an hour.

events.text: Theron Kell has drawn a circle on the gold floor that is half rune and half array, the two scripts braided. It does not work. "It nearly works," he says, haggard. "If it works, it means our two skies are one sky, seen from two sides. If it does not, I wasted my life." He hands you a stick of chalk. "Fight me first. Then help me."

choices.text: Help him find what is missing

effects.log: It is the letters: the third script, the mason's, at the edge of the floor. You show him. He stares at them for a long time. "Someone already did it," he whispers. "Long ago."

choices.text: Tell him a life spent asking is not wasted

effects.log: He laughs, tired. "You are a terrible scientist and a very good friend." He fights you with the half-working circle, and it nearly works.

choices.text: Solve the braided circle with him

effects.log: With Geum-ha beside you, the three of you push the circle round, and for one breath it hums. Theron sits down on the gold, laughing and laughing.

events.text: Theron Kell is packing his rune circles into a satchel. Geum-ha is untied, sitting on his cushion, pouring tea for the archmage. "I am going home," Theron says. "To write the paper. Nobody will believe it." He straightens. "One last fight, for the record. Then I give your grandmaster his floor back, with interest."

choices.text: Fight him for the record, and win

effects.log: You win, cleanly, and he writes the result in his notebook with great satisfaction, as if being beaten were a good experimental result. Then he leaves Geum-ha a page of runes.

choices.text: Fight him for the record, and lose

effects.log: He wins and writes that down too, scrupulously. "Data," he says. "All of it is data." He leaves you a page of runes as well, for the next attempt.

choices.text: Ask him to write to you

effects.log: "Letters," he says. "Between the skies. Through the Keeper." He looks thrilled at the idea. "I shall send you a hybrid array. It will probably explode."

choices.text: Pour him a last cup of the grandmaster's tea

effects.log: He drinks it slowly, eyes closed. "Roasted," he says. "I will never find it on my side. That is the only sad part."

events.text: In another life a letter comes in violet ink, with a little array drawn on the back that is half rune and half square. It does not explode. On the seventieth floor, Theron Kell and Geum-ha are drinking tea over a braided circle, and they both look up. "Ah," says Theron. "Our third view."

choices.text: Solve their newest problem

effects.log: It takes all day and three pots of tea. All three of you are delighted with it.

choices.text: Fight Theron for the record

effects.log: He wins or loses and writes it down either way.

events.text: Someone in goggles and a leather apron full of brass tools is crouched by the door of the seventieth floor, tinkering. A small clockwork bird sits on their shoulder, its wings made of brass leaves. "Quill Hartwell," they say, without looking up. "Artificer. Other sky. My bird can read something on that floor. Letters, it says. Shall we go in?" The brass badge on the apron is the cog of the Hartwell Artificers' Guild.

choices.text: Go in, and let the bird look

effects.log: Inside, the bird hops along the gold lines and stops at the letters by the wall, chirping. "It knows them," Quill says, astonished. "Those are from my side of the sky."

choices.text: Ask how a bird can read

effects.log: "Badly," Quill says, delighted to be asked. "It was built to read engine plates. Letters are letters." The bird ticks smugly.

choices.text: Ask Quill to stay at the door, where it is safe

effects.log: "Nowhere is safe," Quill says. "That is why I bring tools." They follow you in anyway, and spend the whole fight fixing things.

events.text: Quill Hartwell has a half-built device on the landing, all brass gears and, of all things, a bead from the golden abacus. "Your grandmaster gave it to me," Quill says. "I am building a thing that reads arrays and turns them into gears. Help me finish it, and we can take the floor together."

choices.text: Help them build it

effects.log: You do the array part; Quill does the gears. The thing clicks and hums and, for a whole minute, moves the gold lines by itself. Geum-ha nearly falls off his cushion.

choices.text: Tune the gears to your own qi

ok.log: The device sings when you touch it. Quill stares at the dials. "It likes you," they say. "Machines never like anyone."

fail.log: A spring jumps out and hits Quill on the nose. "Data," they say, muffled. "All good data."

choices.text: Tell them to keep it simple

effects.log: "Simple," Quill says, as if it were a foreign word. They take three gears out. It works better. They are furious about it, happily.

events.text: After the seventieth floor Quill Hartwell holds the clockwork bird out to you in both hands. "It wants to go with you," they say. "I asked it. For one life. Then it will fly home through the seam." The bird looks at you with its little glass eyes and ticks.

choices.text: Take the bird with you

effects.log: It rides on your shoulder all the way down the Tower. For the rest of this life it will sit in your window and read anything with letters on it, badly, aloud.

choices.text: Tell Quill to keep it

effects.log: Quill looks relieved and ashamed at once. "I would miss it," they admit. The bird sulks, then sits on your hand for one minute before going back.

choices.text: Give Quill something to carry home in its place

effects.log: You give them a plain jade bead. They fit it into the bird's chest, where a heart would be. "Now it has something from both sides," they say.

events.text: A clockwork bird lands on the rail of the gold stair, ticking, and reads the nearest sign aloud in a tinny voice, badly. Behind it comes Quill Hartwell, goggles pushed up, grey in their hair now. "It found you," they say. "It always does. Shall we go in? I have a new device. It probably works."

choices.text: Go in with them and the bird

effects.log: The device works for nearly the whole floor. Quill counts that as a triumph.

choices.text: Ask what the bird has read lately

effects.log: "Everything," says Quill. "Mostly menus." The bird reads you one, proudly.

events.text: One winter night the clockwork bird in your window stops reading the shop signs across the street, turns its glass eyes west, and ticks very fast. It is time, it seems. The seam is calling it home.

choices.text: Open the window

effects.log: It flies out into the snow, west, toward the Tower. In the morning there is one brass leaf on the sill.

choices.text: Hold it a moment longer, then open the window

effects.log: It lets you. Then it reads you the word on your door, badly, aloud, and goes.

events.text: The eightieth floor is a white jade hall open to the sky. An ancient sage with a white beard down to the floor sits ringed by sixteen small jade plaques that float and turn, each with one Dao on it. "Mu-yeom," the sage says. "Which Dao do you love best?" When you answer, one plaque stops in front of you, and the sage speaks its opposite, and the opposite comes for you.

choices.text: Answer the opposite with your own Dao

effects.log: You answer it in the Dao you walk, and keep answering, round after round. The sage takes notes in sixteen colours. "Loyal," the sage says. "Loyal is a beginning."

choices.text: Answer the opposite with the opposite

effects.log: You turn and speak in the Dao against your own. It is clumsy and honest. The sage stops writing. "Few try," they say. "Fewer try well."

choices.text: Ask why the opposite

effects.log: "Because a Dao you have never been argued out of," says the sage, "is only a habit."

events.text: The eightieth floor is a white jade hall open to the sky. An ancient sage with a white beard down to the floor sits ringed by sixteen small jade plaques that float and turn, each with one Dao on it. "Mu-yeom," the sage says. "You walk no Dao yet. Then pick a plaque, any plaque. I will speak it, and you will answer as you can."

choices.text: Pick the plaque that frightens you most

effects.log: It is the Dao of Death. The sage speaks it gently. You answer as well as someone can who has never walked it. "Brave," says the sage. "Answer with that, for now."

choices.text: Pick the plaque nearest you

effects.log: It is the Dao of Water. The sage speaks it, and you answer by stepping aside like water, by luck more than understanding. The sage laughs. "Luck is a small Dao too."

choices.text: Ask the sage to choose for you

effects.log: The sage chooses the Dao of Balance, and answers it for you, in your own voice, while you listen. You learn more from hearing it than from any fight.

events.text: Mu-yeom has set one plaque down on the white jade, in front of you. "Teach me this one," the sage says. "The Dao you walk. As if I knew nothing. A teacher learns what a Dao really is only by trying to give it away."

choices.text: Teach it plainly, as you learned it

effects.log: You teach it like a beginner's lesson, the first steps first. The sage listens like a child. At the end they say, "Now I know how it looks from below," and bow.

choices.text: Teach it as you understand it now, deep and strange

ok.log: You find words for things you had only felt. The sage's note turns a new colour on the page. "There," they say softly. "You just took a step in it yourself."

fail.log: The words do not come. You go round in circles. The sage pats your hand. "That is how you know where the edge of it is," they say.

choices.text: Tell the sage you cannot teach what you have not mastered

effects.log: "Nobody has mastered any of them," says the sage. "Teach what you have." So you do, and it is more than you thought.

events.text: Mu-yeom holds out a plaque. "You still walk no Dao," the sage says. "Then teach me your life instead. A life is a Dao nobody has named. Begin wherever you like."

choices.text: Tell the sage about your hardest year

effects.log: You tell it. The sage writes a note in a colour you have not seen them use before. "Endurance," they say. "That is a plaque I do not have."

choices.text: Tell the sage about your happiest day

effects.log: You tell it. The sage smiles through the beard. "The Dao of Ordinary Joy," they say. "Heaven never wrote it down. It should have."

events.text: Mu-yeom is halfway through speaking a Dao when the word stops. Not the sage: the word. All sixteen plaques freeze in midair. The open sky above the white hall is very still, and very close, and listening. The sage does not move. A long time later they breathe out. "Heaven," they whisper. "It does that here. It has never done it while I was speaking."

choices.text: Say one thing into the silence

effects.log: You say it, quietly. Nobody answers. But the plaques begin to turn again, one by one, as if something heard and was thinking about it.

choices.text: Stay silent with the sage

effects.log: You stay silent. The sky listens to the two of you saying nothing, and then it goes back to being sky. The sage takes your hand, and their hand is shaking.

choices.text: Ask the sage if they are all right

effects.log: "No," says the sage honestly. "I have spoken sixteen Daos for longer than your Tower has had a name, and I just found out somebody was listening." They laugh, unsteadily.

events.text: Mu-yeom sits without the plaques today; they lie stacked on the floor like tiles. "I asked Heaven a question once," the sage says. "Long ago, when I first mastered all sixteen. I asked whether any of them were true. It did not answer. I have been speaking its Daos to climbers ever since, hoping one of you would get an answer for me."

choices.text: Ask what answer the sage hopes for

effects.log: "That one of them is true," says the sage, "or that none of them is, and that is fine too." They smile. "I am not fussy. I would just like to be told."

choices.text: Promise to ask Heaven for them, if you ever can

effects.log: The sage looks at you with very old eyes. "Climbers make that promise," they say. "Some keep it. I have a feeling about you." They set the plaques turning again.

choices.text: Tell the sage the not-answering might be the answer

effects.log: They are silent a long time. "That is a very cruel thing to say," they say at last, "and possibly correct." They fight you very hard after that, and better.

events.text: Mu-yeom holds out a jade plaque to you in both hands. It is the sixteenth, and it is blank. "The Daos are fifteen and a space," the sage says. "I always said sixteen, out of politeness. Your own word goes there. Not now. When you know it." The white hall is open to the sky, and the sky, today, seems to be smiling.

choices.text: Take the blank plaque

effects.log: It is cool and light. In every life after this one you will carry it, and some days you will almost know what goes on it.

choices.text: Ask what word the sage would put there

effects.log: "Mine?" The sage laughs. "Mine would be 'still asking'. Do not copy me. Find your own."

choices.text: Set it back among the fifteen, blank, until you know

effects.log: You set it back in the ring, blank. The sage nods. "Patient," they say. "That is nearly a word already."

events.text: Fifteen plaques turn round the White Sage, and a gap where the sixteenth should be. "You have it," Mu-yeom says. You have met here {tw_chapter} times. "Is there a word on it yet? No? Good. Hurry is a Dao I do not teach. Answer me in your own."

choices.text: Answer in your own Dao

effects.log: Round after round. The sage writes your notes in a colour they keep for you alone.

choices.text: Ask whether Heaven has listened again

effects.log: "Twice," says the sage. "Both times when you were here." They do not seem to find that strange anymore.

events.text: The white jade hall is burning and freezing at once. A man in robes of four colours stands in the middle, fire in one palm and frost in the other, stones floating round him. Mu-yeom's sixteen plaques lie scattered and still. "Aurelian Vos," the man says. "Elementalist. I came to master every element of two worlds." He glances at the plaques, and away. "These frighten me. Fight me and they will stay on the floor." The four colours are the house colours of House Vos of the Four Winds.

choices.text: Fight his four elements with one Dao

effects.log: His fire and frost and stone and wind come at you all at once, and you answer with one thing, steadily. He is unnerved. "One?" he says. "Only one?"

choices.text: Pick up the plaques before the fight

effects.log: You gather them and set them turning again. He backs away from them as if they were hot. "They talk," he says. "Elements do not talk."

choices.text: Ask him why the Daos frighten him

effects.log: "Because an element does what it is," he says, "and a Dao asks what you are." He sets the frost down on the floor, slowly. "I did not like the question."

choices.text: Ask him to set the sage free

effects.log: He looks at the old sage, untouched, simply sitting among fallen plaques. "I did not bind them," he says. "They would not stop talking to me. I only knocked the words down."

events.text: Aurelian Vos holds the white jade hall again, but the plaques are turning, and he is sitting near them, not touching. "The sage spoke to me while I held the floor," he says. "About Water. It is not my water. It moves differently." He looks at you. "Fight me. Then tell me how many Daos there are. Exactly."

choices.text: Tell him sixteen

effects.log: "Sixteen," he says, frustrated. "I have four. Four is a good, sound number." He fights you with all four and loses his temper on the third, which is new for him.

choices.text: Tell him fifteen and a space

effects.log: He stares at the sage, who is smiling. "A space," he says. "A space for what?" "For yours," the sage says. Aurelian does not say anything for a long time.

choices.text: Show him a Dao instead of telling him

effects.log: You move in your Dao, slowly, so he can see it. He watches with fire forgotten in his palm. "That is not an element," he whispers. "That is a person."

events.text: Aurelian Vos asks you before anything else. "I want a seventeenth Dao," he says. "Mine. The Dao of four things that are one thing. Can a person just ask for that? Is it allowed?" Behind him Mu-yeom has stopped the plaques to listen.

choices.text: Tell him a Dao is not asked for, it is walked

effects.log: He looks at his hands, the fire and the frost. "Then I will walk," he says. "Home. And find out what I am on the way." He fights you lightly, after, like someone saying goodbye.

choices.text: Ask the sage to answer him

effects.log: Mu-yeom considers. "It is allowed," the sage says. "Heaven might not listen. I would." Aurelian bows to the old sage so low his stones fall out of the air.

choices.text: Tell him yes, ask it now

effects.log: He asks, aloud, to the open sky. Nothing answers. He laughs, shaking. "It did not say no," he says.

events.text: Aurelian Vos stands at the stair with his four colours dimmed and a small pouch at his belt. "I am going home to the world of four elements," he says. "To find out if the fifth was there all along, under them. One last fight, to see if I am any less afraid." Mu-yeom watches from the turning plaques.

choices.text: Fight him, and see

effects.log: He is less afraid. You can see it in the way he lets the fire and the frost touch instead of keeping them apart. At the end he bows to the sage, and to you, and goes.

choices.text: Give him a plaque to carry home

effects.log: Mu-yeom lets you take the Dao of Earth from the ring. Aurelian holds it as if it might speak. "I will bring it back," he says. "With something in exchange."

choices.text: Ask what is in the pouch

effects.log: "Seeds," he says. "From your gate. I want to see if they grow in a world of four elements." He grins. "If they do, I will send you some of ours."

events.text: In another life a pouch of seeds arrives from nowhere, with no letter. You plant them. They grow into a plant that is somehow fire and frost and stone and air at once, and smells of rain. On the eightieth floor, Aurelian Vos is waiting with the plaque of Earth in his hand. "I brought it back," he says. "Did they grow?"

choices.text: Tell him they grew

effects.log: He is so pleased the stones round him start to float in circles of their own.

choices.text: Fight him, four against one, again

effects.log: He is less afraid than ever. It shows.

events.text: A woman in an antler-crowned hood waits at the white jade door, a staff of living wood in her hand, a red fox at her heel. "Sable Winterbourne," she says. "Druid, from the other sky." She tilts her head toward the hall. "Something in there is singing. The one about trees. I have never heard a song like it." She is of the Winterbourne grove-circle, druids since before their sky had names.

choices.text: Go in and listen with her

effects.log: It is the plaque of the Dao of Wood, turning. Sable stands in front of it with her eyes shut, humming along, and when the sage speaks the Dao of Metal against you she answers it with the song.

choices.text: Tell her it is not a song, it is a Dao

effects.log: "What is the difference?" she asks, interested. You try to explain. Halfway through you realise you are not sure.

choices.text: Ask her fox if it hears it too

effects.log: The fox sits down and looks at the plaque of Wood with its ears forward. Sable laughs. "It does. It is a very musical fox."

events.text: Sable Winterbourne sits on the white jade with her staff across her knees and the fox asleep against her. "A trade," she says. "You give me a Dao, any one, as much as you can say of it. I give you a rite of my grove. Then we fight your sage together."

choices.text: Give her the Dao you walk

effects.log: You tell her what you can. She listens the way trees listen to rain. Then she gives you a rite for asking a forest's leave before you enter it. It is the strangest gift you have ever been given, and it works.

choices.text: Give her the Dao of Wood, since she already hears it

effects.log: She laughs. "Cheat." But she lets you, and teaches you a rite for waking a seed, and the seed in your palm opens before you have finished the words.

choices.text: Tell her you will trade a story instead

effects.log: She agrees, delighted. You tell her a story of your side of the sky; she tells you one of hers. Both are about a tower.

events.text: After the eightieth floor, Sable Winterbourne kneels on the white jade where there is no soil at all, presses a seed into a crack between two tiles, and sings. Her staff puts out leaves. The fox circles three times. "A tree," she says, "that grows in every life after this one, in every Tower. So you know where I have been."

choices.text: Sing with her

effects.log: You do not know the words. You hum. The seed splits, and a pale green shoot comes up out of the jade, and Mu-yeom leans over from the plaques to look at it, delighted.

choices.text: Give it water from your own flask

effects.log: She smiles. "That is the most important part of the rite," she says, "and nobody ever does it."

choices.text: Ask her when she will come back

effects.log: "When it is taller than you," she says. "Then I will know you are still climbing."

events.text: There is a tree growing out of the white jade of the eightieth floor, taller every life, its roots split through the tiles. Under it a druid in an antler hood sits with an old red fox. "It is taller than you now," Sable Winterbourne says. "So I came."

choices.text: Climb the white jade with her again

effects.log: She answers the sage's Daos with songs. You answer with yours. It is a very loud floor.

choices.text: Sit under the tree with her first

effects.log: The fox comes and lies on your feet. Nobody says anything for a long time.

events.text: The ninetieth floor is only cloud. A towering general in storm-black armour stands on it with a halberd that crackles with lightning and a cloak of storm cloud, and behind him nine thunder drums float in the grey. "Noe-gang," he says. "Nine strikes. Stand under them." He does not wait. The first drum sounds, and the first bolt comes down.

choices.text: Stand under all nine without a step back

effects.log: You stand. One, two, three, and the cloud under you shakes. At the end he looks at you, unimpressed. "Standing is the least of it," he says. "Every tree stands."

choices.text: Meet each strike with a counter

effects.log: You strike back at each bolt as it falls, and some of them you break. He raises one eyebrow. "Defiance," he says. "Expensive. Keep it."

choices.text: Count the strikes aloud as they come

effects.log: You count, steadily, through all of them. He listens to the counting more than he watches the fight. "Nine," he says, at the end. "I will remember how many."

choices.text: Get up off the cloud

effects.log: He watches you get up. "Five," he says. "You survived five. I keep count of every life." He sounds neither pleased nor sorry.

events.text: The nine drums sound, and the lightning of the ninetieth floor takes shapes as it falls: faint human figures over the cloud. You know them. They are people you failed, one for each strike. The Thunder Marshal stands among them with his halberd lowered. "Your regrets," he says. "I read them, to choose the shapes. Stand under them."

choices.text: Name each one as it strikes

effects.log: You name them aloud, one per bolt. It hurts more than the lightning. At the end the Marshal is looking at you in a new way. "Nobody names them," he says.

choices.text: Stand under them in silence

effects.log: You say nothing and you do not step aside. The faint figures pass through you like rain. When it is over there is one less weight on you, and you do not know which.

choices.text: Ask him to strike with something else

effects.log: "No," he says. "This is the strike you are afraid of. That is the only kind I have."

events.text: The nine drums sound, and the lightning of the ninetieth floor takes shapes as it falls: faint human figures over the cloud. They are blurred, people you might have failed if you had lived differently. The Thunder Marshal frowns at them. "You carry few regrets," he says. "So I strike with the ones you are lucky not to have."

choices.text: Stand under them and be grateful

effects.log: You stand, and thank each one quietly as it passes. The Marshal does not understand it. He strikes harder, and you go on thanking them.

choices.text: Ask him whether he carries regrets

effects.log: He is silent through three strikes. "Only one," he says. "Ask me another life."

events.text: The Thunder Marshal lowers his halberd before the first drum. The cloud is very quiet. "Why do you climb?" he asks. "Every climber who reaches me is asked by me to stand under nine strikes. Nobody has ever asked me why I strike. So I will ask you first."

choices.text: Tell him the truth, whatever it is

effects.log: You tell him. He listens all the way through without moving. Then he raises the halberd, and the strikes that follow are as hard as ever, and somehow fairer.

choices.text: Ask him why he strikes

effects.log: He opens his mouth and nothing comes out. The drums behind him are silent. "I do not know," he says at last, very quietly. "Nobody has asked me in ten thousand years."

choices.text: Tell him: because nobody said I could

effects.log: He laughs, once, like thunder far off. "That," he says, "is the only answer Heaven fears." The strikes come anyway.

events.text: The nine drums stay silent. Noe-gang walks to you across the cloud, the lightning dying along his halberd, and kneels. He lays the halberd down. Above him, for the first time, the clouds clear. "I am Heaven's fear," he says, "given armour. It made me to stop the one who will reach the top. I have stood here so long that I do not want to win anymore."

choices.text: Tell him to stand up

effects.log: He stands. He is very tall and very tired. "Then I will strike you because I choose to," he says, "and not because I was made to." It is the first free strike he has ever thrown.

choices.text: Kneel with him
