effects.log: You kneel across from him on the cloud. In the clear sky above there is nothing but light. "Heaven is watching," he says. "Let it."

choices.text: Ask what Heaven hopes for, if it is afraid

effects.log: He looks up at the clear sky. "That someone will do it anyway," he says. "Fear and hope are the same strike, from either end."

events.text: Noe-gang takes the ninth drum down from the grey air with both hands. It is small for a thunder drum, and very old, and it hums. He holds it out to you. "Strike it when Heaven is wrong," he says. "Only then. It will answer."

choices.text: Take the drum

effects.log: You take it. It is heavier than it looks, and lighter than it should be. In every life after this one you will feel it near you, waiting for the day Heaven is wrong.

choices.text: Ask how you will know Heaven is wrong

effects.log: "You will know," he says. "Everyone always knows. That is the trouble." He folds your hands round the drum.

choices.text: Strike it once now, gently, to hear it

effects.log: It sounds once, low, and somewhere very far above the Tower the sky goes quiet to listen. The Marshal smiles for the first time. "Not yet," he says. "But good."

events.text: Eight drums float behind the Thunder Marshal, and a gap where the ninth should be. "You still have it," Noe-gang says. You have met here {tw_chapter} times. "Good. I strike now because I choose to. Stand under it, if you choose to."

choices.text: Choose to stand under it

effects.log: Eight strikes. Each one free, each one fair. You stand.

choices.text: Ask him what he does between climbers

effects.log: "I watch the clouds," he says. "They used to look like armies. Now they look like clouds."

events.text: The ninetieth floor roars. A great blue storm-drake wheels through the lightning, and on its back sits a knight in blue steel with a winged helm and a long lance. The Thunder Marshal kneels in the cloud, his halberd broken. "Ysolde Kestrel," the knight calls down. "Dragon-knight. I came to fight a god. This one was only armour." She turns the drake toward you. "Are you a god?" Her winged helm is the helm of the Kestrel drakeriders of Highcrag.

choices.text: Tell her no, and fight her anyway

effects.log: The drake dives and you meet the lance on the cloud. She is the best rider you have ever seen, and you are not a god, and it is the fight of your life.

choices.text: Fight the drake, not the rider

effects.log: You take the drake's charge and turn it gently, again and again, until it lands on the cloud and folds its wings. Ysolde slides down, furious and fascinated. "It likes you," she says.

choices.text: Tell her yes: you are one, in this life

effects.log: Her helm comes off. She looks at you a long time. "Then this is the fight I crossed the sky for," she says, and couches the lance.

choices.text: Help the Marshal to his feet

effects.log: He takes your arm. Ysolde watches from the saddle. "He would not fight me with his whole heart," she says. "You did."

events.text: Ysolde Kestrel holds the cloud floor again. The drake is lying on the cloud with its head on its forelegs, and she is sitting against its side, polishing the lance. "In my sky," she says, "a knight who fights a god and wins becomes a story forever. I wanted to be a story." She looks at you. "Is that a bad reason?"

choices.text: Tell her it is a lonely reason

effects.log: She is quiet. "The drake would agree," she says. The drake opens one eye. She fights you after with less fury and more skill.

choices.text: Tell her every climber here wants something like that

effects.log: "Even you?" she asks. You tell her the truth. She laughs. "Then we are both bad people," she says cheerfully, and mounts.

choices.text: Ask the drake's name

effects.log: She says it, a long rolling word. The drake lifts its great head at its name and looks at you with an eye like a storm lantern.

events.text: Ysolde Kestrel does not mount the drake today. "I asked your Marshal," she says, "while I held this floor. Who made him. He said: Heaven, out of fear. So I came to fight a god, and found a god's fear instead." She looks at the Marshal, kneeling, unbroken. "I do not want to fight fear. Help me find out what I want."

choices.text: Tell her to fight for someone, not against something

effects.log: She thinks of someone; you can see it in her face. "My squire," she says. "Back home. Waiting." She fights you that day as if the squire were watching.

choices.text: Fight her until she knows

effects.log: You fight her, hard, until she laughs in the middle of it. "Oh," she says. "I want this. Just this. A good fight with a good person." She sounds astonished.

choices.text: Ask the Marshal to answer her

effects.log: Noe-gang looks up. "I was made to want nothing," he says. "Do not copy me." Ysolde bows to him from the saddle, deeply.

events.text: Ysolde Kestrel lowers her lance before the drake and bows from the saddle. "I give this floor back to its Marshal," she says. "One last pass, for honour, and then I fly home through the seam, and I will tell them I met no god, only the best fighter on either side of it."

choices.text: Take the pass, and win

effects.log: You meet the lance on the cloud and turn it, and the drake banks away with her laughing on its back. From the clouds below you hear her shout something in her own tongue that sounds like praise.

choices.text: Take the pass, and fall

effects.log: She catches you on the drake's tail before you go through the cloud. "Not today," she says, and sets you down gently. "Next life. I insist."

choices.text: Ask her to carry a message to the other side

effects.log: "To whom?" she asks. "Anyone who climbs," you say. "Tell them the Tower is one Tower." She salutes with the lance. "I will."

choices.text: Touch the drake's nose in farewell

effects.log: It breathes over you, warm as a summer storm. Ysolde watches, pleased. "It will remember you," she says. "Drakes remember longer than knights."

events.text: In another life a great blue scale, shed and shining, is found on your roof one morning after a storm. On the ninetieth floor the storm-drake bugles when it sees you, and Ysolde Kestrel, older, with a scar on her cheek, grins from the saddle. "It insisted," she says. "It always insists."

choices.text: Take a pass with her, for old times

effects.log: Lance and arts, the cloud and the drake. Nobody wins. Everybody laughs.

choices.text: Thank the drake for the scale

effects.log: It bows its great head. Ysolde has never seen it bow to anyone.

events.text: A big man in a grey cassock with mail beneath it waits at the cloud stair, a silver storm-sign in his fist. "Rowan Hale," he booms. "Battle-priest of the tempest, from the other sky." He squints at the thunder above. "That is a tribulation. I know a prayer for those. Let me pray it smaller for you." His sign is the silver bolt of the Tempest Chapter of Hale.

choices.text: Let him pray

effects.log: He prays in a voice like rain on a roof. The nine strikes still come, but each one is a little smaller than it would have been, and you stand under them better.

choices.text: Tell him to save his prayer for himself

effects.log: "Nonsense," he roars. "A prayer is not money. It does not run out." He prays anyway, for both of you.

choices.text: Ask what his god is like

effects.log: "Loud," he says, grinning. "Generous. Bad at keeping appointments." He shrugs. "Like me."

events.text: The seventh strike of the ninetieth floor comes down at you, the worst of the nine, and Rowan Hale steps under it beside you with his silver sign raised, shouting a prayer into the light. It hits you both. You are both still standing when it is gone, smoking a little.

choices.text: Thank him

effects.log: "Do not," he says, coughing. "A priest who will not stand under the storm with his people is only a man who talks to the sky." He thumps your back. "Two more."

choices.text: Stand closer for the eighth

effects.log: You stand shoulder to shoulder for the eighth and the ninth. Between you, the storm finds less to hit.

choices.text: Tell him he is mad

effects.log: "Of course," he says, delighted. "The tempest likes the mad ones." He laughs so hard the Marshal looks over.

events.text: After the ninetieth floor Rowan Hale sits on the edge of the cloud with his storm-sign in his lap. "I will give you my prayer," he says. "The one for tribulations. Not for you. For your people, whoever they are. Say it over them when their storms come."

choices.text: Learn the prayer, word by word

effects.log: He teaches it slowly. It is in his tongue, and you get the sounds wrong, and he says that does not matter at all. "The tempest is not fussy about accents."

choices.text: Teach him a breath for standing under storms in return

effects.log: He learns it badly and loudly. "Ha!" he shouts at the next roll of thunder. "That one barely tickled."

choices.text: Ask him to say it over you once, now

effects.log: He puts his big hand on your head and says it. Somewhere, very faintly, thunder answers in a voice like rain on a roof.

events.text: You hear him before you reach the cloud stair: a voice like rain on a roof, praying. Rowan Hale is there, grey in his beard, mail patched. "My people say the prayer now," he booms. "Do yours?" He raises the silver sign. "Come. Nine strikes. Smaller."

choices.text: Stand under the storm with him again

effects.log: Shoulder to shoulder. The storm finds less to hit.

choices.text: Say his prayer back to him

effects.log: You still get the sounds wrong. He laughs until the Marshal looks over.

events.text: The ninety-ninth floor is a single stone in a sea of white mist, and there is no bell at the eave above it. A small elderly nun in pale grey stands on the stone with a closed paper fan. She bows. You never hear a footstep. You never feel her qi. You never see the fan move. You only find yourself, again and again, somewhere other than where you were.

choices.text: Stop listening for her, and listen to nothing

effects.log: You stop trying to hear her and listen to the silence itself. Somewhere in it is the shape of a fan. She bows again, very slightly.

choices.text: Trust your feet: they have climbed ninety-eight floors

effects.log: Your feet remember every floor below. They move before you do. Twice they move right, and the mist where you were is cut in two.

choices.text: Bow back, and wait for her to move

effects.log: You bow and do not move. Nothing happens for a very long time. Then she is beside you, and touches your shoulder with the fan, and it is over, one way or the other.

events.text: The Mute Abbess stands on her stone, and at her feet there is a row of small pebbles, very neat, all the way to the edge of the mist. She points at them with the closed fan, and then at you. One for each attempt, the gesture says, across every life. There are more than you thought.

choices.text: Count the pebbles

effects.log: You count them. You stop counting at {tw_climbs} climbs and pebbles, not because you run out, but because it does not matter. She nods, as if that were the right number.

choices.text: Add a pebble of your own

effects.log: You find a pebble in your sleeve from the gate below and set it at the end of the row. She looks at it a long time. Then she smiles, and does not say anything.

choices.text: Ask her, with your hands, why she keeps them

effects.log: She opens her hands, then closes them round nothing, and holds them to her chest. Because you came, the gesture says. Because you kept coming.

events.text: The Mute Abbess opens her paper fan for the first time. There is writing on it, in faded ink, in a hand you have seen before: on the Tower's gate posts, on the Keeper's cup, on the tablets of the first floor. She turns it so you can read the last line. "For my last apprentice, who will hear what I cannot say."

choices.text: Bow to her as the Keeper's apprentice

effects.log: You bow deeply. She bows back, deeper. For a moment the mist on the ninety-ninth floor smells of barley tea.

choices.text: Ask her what the Keeper could not say

effects.log: She closes the fan and points down, the whole height of the Tower, to the gate. Then she puts a finger to her own lips. Ask them, it says. Not me. Not yet.

choices.text: Read the whole fan

effects.log: She lets you. It is instructions for sweeping a stair, and a recipe for tea, and at the end, very small, a name crossed out and written again. You cannot quite read it.

events.text: The Mute Abbess does not raise her fan today. She steps toward you across the stone, close, and for the first time in all your lives, she speaks. Only one word. It is a name: Ha Seol-jong. Her voice is very small and very clear. Far below, at the gate of the Tower, a broom stops sweeping.

choices.text: Repeat the name, as quietly as she said it

effects.log: You say it back. She closes her eyes. Somewhere below, the broom begins again, slower, as if the person holding it were listening.

choices.text: Carry the name down to the gate

effects.log: At the gate you only say it once. The Keeper does not look up. "Not this floor," they say, very gently, and then, "Thank you."

choices.text: Keep the name in silence, as she did

effects.log: You do not say it. She sees that you will not, and bows, and for the rest of the climb your footsteps make no sound.

events.text: The Mute Abbess stands on her stone and looks at you for a long time. Then she steps aside, off the stone, onto the mist, and does not fall. She points up with the closed fan. Above the ninety-ninth floor, where there has never been anything but mist, there is a stair of light, and at its top a door that has no lock.

choices.text: Look at the door

effects.log: You look. Words form on the door and fade before you can read them, all but one line: what Heaven still waits to see. A list. Your list. The Abbess nods, and goes back to her stone.

choices.text: Bow to her before anything else

effects.log: You bow. She bows back, and then, very quietly, she laughs: a small sound, the only one she has ever made but the name.

choices.text: Ask her to come up with you, one day

effects.log: She shakes her head and points at her pebbles, at the gate, at you. Someone has to keep count, the gesture says. Go.

events.text: The Mute Abbess stands on her stone in the mist. There is one more pebble at the end of the row than there was. Above, the stair of light waits, and the door with no lock. She does not move. She never moves where you can see.

choices.text: Climb past her into the silence

effects.log: You never hear a thing. That is how you know it went right.

choices.text: Add your pebble to the row

effects.log: She watches you set it down, and smiles.

events.text: There is no sound on the ninety-ninth floor, and a white mask in the mist. The Mute Abbess sits on the edge of her stone, unhurt and unbothered. On it stands a figure in dark grey hooded leathers with twin short blades. She moves without a sound, like the Abbess, but not as well. Nobody speaks. She raises the blades. On her glove is the plain grey knot of the Hushed Guild of Morrow.

choices.text: Fight her in her own silence

effects.log: Two silent fighters on a stone in the mist. You can hear her breathing, just; she cannot hear yours at all. The Abbess watches, interested, from the edge.

choices.text: Make a sound on purpose

effects.log: You strike your heel on the stone. It rings like a bell. The masked figure flinches as if struck. Whatever she climbed here to escape, it is sound.

choices.text: Sit down beside the Abbess and wait

effects.log: You sit. After a long while the masked figure lowers her blades, confused, and sits too, a little way off.

events.text: The nightblade holds the silent floor again, mask on, blades out. When she sees you she does not attack. She pulls a scrap of paper from her sleeve and writes on it, and holds it out: Ilsabet Morrow. Then, underneath: I heard there was a place where no one can hear you weep.

choices.text: Write back: they can still see you

effects.log: You write it and hand it over. She reads it, and her shoulders shake under the hood. She does not raise the blades again that day.

choices.text: Write back: then weep, and fight me after

effects.log: She does, there, in silence, for a long time. Then she stands and fights you, quick and clean, and better than before.

choices.text: Tell her aloud, gently, that you would hear it

effects.log: She stares at you through the mask. Nobody has spoken to her in a long time. She writes: why? You do not have an answer that fits on paper.

events.text: Ilsabet Morrow has taken off her white mask. Her face is ordinary and very tired. She writes on her paper: the Abbess has not spoken to me either. Not one word. I thought that was what I wanted. She looks at the old nun, who is looking at nothing. Then she writes: fight me, and I will try to say something.

choices.text: Fight her, and listen for the word

effects.log: It comes at the very end, when her blades are down and her breath is gone. One word, hoarse: "Thank you." It is the first thing she has said in years.

choices.text: Tell her she does not have to say anything

effects.log: She looks relieved and sad at once. She writes: I want to. That is the trouble. She tries, and cannot yet, and is not ashamed of it.

choices.text: Ask the Abbess to help her

effects.log: The Abbess opens her fan and shows Ilsabet the last line. Ilsabet reads it several times. Then she writes: so she can speak. She just saves it.

events.text: Ilsabet Morrow is waiting at the edge of the mist with her mask in her hand. "I am going home," she says aloud. Her voice is rough from disuse, and she winces at it, and keeps going. "One last fight. Then I will find someone to talk to. Out loud. About everything."

choices.text: Fight her, and win

effects.log: She fights well and loses well, and laughs out loud at the end, startled by the sound. She gives the floor back to the Abbess with a bow.

choices.text: Fight her, and lose

effects.log: She wins, and says, "Again?" aloud, and then claps a hand over her mouth, laughing.

choices.text: Ask her who she will talk to first

effects.log: "My mother," she says, "if she is still alive. She used to sing." She puts the mask in your hands. "Keep it. I will not need it."

choices.text: Promise to be someone she can talk to

effects.log: "In which life?" she asks, half laughing. "Any," you say. She nods slowly. "Then I will keep watch for you," she says, "in one of them."

events.text: In another life there is a dangerous year, and every night of it you sleep well. Once you wake and see a figure in dark grey on your roof, keeping watch, unmasked. On the ninety-ninth floor Ilsabet Morrow waits at the edge of the mist. "You slept well," she says aloud. "I made sure."

choices.text: Thank her, aloud

effects.log: She grins. "Say it louder," she says. "I like hearing things now."

choices.text: Fight her in the silence, for old times

effects.log: Neither of you makes a sound. Both of you are smiling.

events.text: In the white mist of the ninety-ninth floor, where nothing burns and nothing sounds, there is a light: a brass lantern on a long pole, held by a gentle man in a long coat. "Wil Vael," he says. "Lamplighter of the grey road, on the other side. My lantern burns here. Nothing else does. Shall I light your way?" His coat bears the lamp of House Vael, lamplighters of the grey road.

choices.text: Walk in his light

effects.log: In his small circle of light the mist shows you where the Abbess is, just for a breath, before she moves. It is enough. He grins. "It has never been useful before," he says.

choices.text: Ask why his lantern burns here

effects.log: "Family thing," he says. "We always kept a tower, somewhere west. Kept the lamps lit. I think it remembers us."

events.text: Wil Vael sets his lantern down on the Abbess's stone and sits beside it. "My family has a story," he says. "An ancestor of ours, a stonewright, went to the edge of the world and came home, years later, and never said what was there. Only that she had left half of something unfinished, and someone was keeping it." He looks up at the mist. "I think it is this."

choices.text: Tell him about the letters on the gold floor

effects.log: He listens with his mouth open. "Letters," he says. "Our letters. In your tower." He laughs and puts his face in his hands. "She was here. She was really here."

choices.text: Ask what she was like

effects.log: "Stubborn," he says. "Laid stones without asking anyone. The family says I have her hands." He holds them out. They are a stonewright's hands, holding a lamplighter's pole.

choices.text: Tell him the Keeper speaks of a friend

effects.log: He goes very still. "A friend," he says. "From the east. She called them that too." The lantern flame stands straight up in the windless mist.

events.text: Wil Vael lifts his lantern high, and in the mist above the ninety-ninth floor its light finds a stair: not of stone, not of wood, but of light, going up to a door with no lock. "Someone on my side," he says softly, "is waiting for this door to open. I think they always have been." He hands you the lantern pole to hold, just for a moment.

choices.text: Hold the lantern and look up

effects.log: It is warm. The stair of light holds steady while you hold it. When you give it back, Wil is smiling and trying not to cry.

choices.text: Promise to open it one day

effects.log: "I believe you," he says, simply. "My family has a word for that. It means: the lamp is lit, the road is long, come anyway."

choices.text: Ask him to wait for you at the top

effects.log: "At the west door," he says. "Always." He knocks the pole on the stone twice, like a vow.

events.text: A brass lantern burns in the mist of the ninety-ninth floor, where nothing else burns. Wil Vael is holding it, older now, with a stonewright's hands. "Your way," he says, and lifts it. "As always."

choices.text: Walk in his light again

effects.log: The Abbess is a breath slower in it, and you are a breath faster.

choices.text: Look up at the stair of light together

effects.log: It is still there, and the door is still waiting. Neither of you says anything.

events.text: Between two floors of the upper Tower, on a landing where you have never seen anyone, a brass lantern burns on a long pole. A gentle man in a long coat is holding it, and looking at the stairs ahead the way a traveller looks at weather. "Oh," he says, "a climber. From the east of the seam. Wil Vael. Lamplighter. Shall we take the next floor together? Mine has been very lonely."

choices.text: Take the floor together

effects.log: He fights with the lantern pole like a quarterstaff, badly and bravely, and his light shows you things the floor meant to hide. At the top of the stair he shakes your hand twice, like a western contract.

choices.text: Ask him what he fights with, on his side

effects.log: "Rites," he says. "Little ones. A lamp-rite, a door-rite, a rite for not getting lost." He shows you one. It is very like an array, and nothing like one.

choices.text: Climb on alone, politely

effects.log: He bows, unoffended. "Another floor, then," he says. "I keep finding people on these stairs. I will probably find you."

events.text: Wil Vael is on the landing again, lantern lit, and he is arguing before you reach him. "I have been thinking," he says, "about your qi. It is a lamp you light inside yourself, yes? Then my rites are better. A lamp should be outside, where other people can see by it." He plants the pole. "Prove me wrong. Floor and argument, both."

choices.text: Argue that a lamp inside lights the one who carries it

effects.log: "And who lights the road?" he says. "The road lights itself, if enough people walk it," you say. He opens his mouth, closes it, and laughs. "Draw," he says.

choices.text: Spar with him, arts against rites

effects.log: Your arts against his rites, on a narrow landing, both of you laughing. He loses, cheerfully, and insists that the floor was tilted.

choices.text: Concede that his lamp is kinder

effects.log: He looks at you suspiciously. "That is a trap," he says. "An eastern trap." It is not, and he knows it, and he is pleased all the way up the next stair.

events.text: The floor throws you, hard, toward the open edge of the stairwell, and there is nothing to hold. Then there is: a brass lantern pole, hooked through your belt, and Wil Vael on the other end of it, both boots braced on the rail. "Got you," he says through his teeth. "Got you. Do not move. Please do not move."

choices.text: Hold still and let him pull you in

effects.log: He pulls you in, inch by inch, and sits down hard on the landing when it is done, shaking. "That," he says, "is the worst thing that has ever happened to a lamp."

choices.text: Thank him, when you can breathe

effects.log: "Do not thank me," he says. "Teach me how you fell so well. I would have broken in three places." He is still holding the pole as if you might go over again.

choices.text: Tell him he should not have risked it

effects.log: "Should not?" He looks honestly confused. "You were falling. What else is a lamp for?"

events.text: You win the floor, but in the last moment something comes at your back that you do not see. Wil Vael does. He steps into it with the lantern held high, and it strikes the brass and him together, and the light goes out for the first time since you have known him. He sits on the floor in the dark. "Ow," he says. "Somebody relight me."

choices.text: Relight his lantern with your own qi

effects.log: You hold your hand to the wick and push. It catches, a little bluer than before. He stares at it. "Now it is half yours," he says. "That cannot be undone. Good."

choices.text: Help him up and check his ribs

effects.log: They are bruised, not broken. He grumbles the whole time you check. "Lamps," he says, "are not meant to be shields. Do not tell my family."

choices.text: Tell him he saved you

effects.log: "Did I?" He beams in the dark. "Good. I have been wanting to do that for three floors."

events.text: Wil Vael is waiting on the landing with his lantern set down and his coat brushed. He looks nervous, which you have never seen. "On my side," he says, "people who keep finding each other on the road swear a vow. Road-kin. On your side, I am told, you have an oath too: under the sky, with wine or water, as sworn kin." He holds out both stonewright's hands. "Across the seam. Both worlds. Will you?"

choices.text: Swear it, the eastern way and his way both

effects.log: You kneel facing west and he kneels facing east, and you say the old oath of sworn kin under the sky, and he says his road-vow, and you share water from his flask because there is no wine. "Kin," he says, trying the word. "Across the worlds. At the top, I will wait at the west door."

choices.text: Swear it simply, in plain words

effects.log: "Kin," you say, and he says it back, and you clasp hands over the lantern flame, and that is all. It is enough. "At the top," he says, "I will wait for you at the west door. Do not make me wait too long."

choices.text: Tell him you are not ready to swear

effects.log: He nods slowly, and picks up his lantern. "Not ready is not no," he says. "My family has a saying: the road is long, and the lamp keeps." He lights your way up the next stair, as always.

events.text: Wil Vael is on the landing again, in another life of yours, his lantern lit. He does not mention the vow. He argues about qi and lamps, as he always does, and fights beside you, and at the top of the stair he looks at you once, quickly, and away.

choices.text: Ask him to swear the vow now

effects.log: His face lights up brighter than the lantern. You kneel, east and west, and swear it, the oath of sworn kin and his road-vow, with water from his flask. "At the west door," he says. "Always."

choices.text: Climb on as friends

effects.log: Friends is a good word too. He says so himself, and means it, and lights the stair.

choices.text: Argue that lamps belong inside, again

effects.log: He is delighted. "Finally," he says. "I was getting bored."

events.text: Your sworn kin from the other sky is on the landing, lantern lit, as if he had been waiting just for you, which he has. "Kin," Wil Vael says, and grins. "The west door is still there. I checked. Shall we argue about lamps, or fight something, or both?"

choices.text: Both, as always

effects.log: You fight the floor and argue the whole way up. Neither of you wins either.

choices.text: Ask how the road is on his side

effects.log: Long, he says. The lamps are lit. People keep finding each other on it. He tells you their names.

choices.text: Let him take a blow, then take one for him

effects.log: He takes one for you; you take the next for him. "Fair," he says. "Kin keep score so they can lose it."

events.text: Brother Odo is waiting on the steps of the red hall with two cups and a jug of water, which for him is solemn. "In my order," he says, "when two people have fought side by side enough times, they swear to be kin. Every hearth of the Open Door would know your name. I would like to swear it with you. Here. Today."

choices.text: Swear kinship with Brother Odo, under both skies

effects.log: You swear it on the red lacquer steps, his way and yours: a cup of water each, a bow to the east, a bow to the west, his laughing prayer and your old oath. "Kin," he says, and laughs so hard he spills the water. "Across the seam!"

choices.text: Tell them you would rather stay friends

effects.log: Brother Odo nods, and does not ask again this life. "Friends," they say. "That is not small either."

choices.text: Ask what the vow means on their side

effects.log: They tell you: a name said at every hearth, a seat kept at every table, a door that is never barred. It is not so different from the east.

events.text: Brother Odo, your sworn kin from the other sky, is on the steps of the red hall with a pot of terrible soup. "Kin!" he booms, and hugs you so hard your ribs complain. "Every friar of the Open Door asks after you. Come, the eastern fist and the friar's fist, together."

choices.text: Fight beside your sworn kin

effects.log: He laughs the whole floor through and takes no blow meant for you that he can reach. You take the ones meant for him.

choices.text: Eat the soup, as kin must

effects.log: It is terrible. You both finish it. That is the vow, he says.

events.text: Elowen Brisk sits at the iron stair with her hawk asleep on her knee. She does not look at you when she speaks, which is how you know it matters. "Wardens swear kin," she says. "Not often. I have never. I would. With you." She pulls out her knife and cuts a strip of green cloth from her hood, and holds it out.

choices.text: Swear kinship with Elowen, under both skies

effects.log: You tie the green strip round your wrist and give her a strip of your own sleeve, and say the old oath of sworn kin under the sky, and she says three words of the Wardens' tongue. The hawk wakes up for it. "Kin," she says. Then, very quietly, "Good."

choices.text: Tell them you would rather stay friends

effects.log: Elowen nods, and does not ask again this life. "Friends," they say. "That is not small either."

choices.text: Ask what the vow means on their side

effects.log: They tell you: a name said at every hearth, a seat kept at every table, a door that is never barred. It is not so different from the east.

events.text: Your sworn kin is at the iron stair: Elowen Brisk, the green strip still round her wrist, faded. Her hawk lands on your arm before she says anything. "Kin," she says, which for her is a speech.

choices.text: Track the floor together

effects.log: She tracks, you fight. You do not need to speak at all.

choices.text: Light a fire first, as kin

effects.log: The hawk sleeps on your arm. Elowen talks, nearly a whole sentence at a time.

events.text: Mira Thistledown stands at the silver door with her holy sign in her hands. "I chose who to be," she says. "Now I would like to choose who to belong to. The Grey Sisters let us swear kin with one person in our lives. Only one. I would like it to be you, if you will have me."

choices.text: Swear kinship with Mira, under both skies

effects.log: She blesses you, and you swear the old oath of sworn kin under the sky, and the Archivist, without being asked, writes it in both your scrolls at once. "Kin," Mira says, and laughs because she is crying. "I will remember this one. I will remember this one."

choices.text: Tell them you would rather stay friends

effects.log: Mira nods, and does not ask again this life. "Friends," they say. "That is not small either."

choices.text: Ask what the vow means on their side

effects.log: They tell you: a name said at every hearth, a seat kept at every table, a door that is never barred. It is not so different from the east.

events.text: Mira Thistledown, your sworn kin, meets you at the silver door. "The Archivist shows me your scroll sometimes," she says. "Only the good parts. It says there are a lot of them." She raises her sign. "Come, kin."

choices.text: Climb the silver floor with your sworn kin

effects.log: She blesses every blow you take, and you take every blow you can for her.

choices.text: Ask what the Archivist wrote

effects.log: "Kin," she says, "in both our hands." She shows you. It is true.

events.text: Rowan Hale sets his silver storm-sign down on the cloud, which he never does. "In the Tempest Chapter," he booms, then lowers his voice, "we swear kin with the ones who stood under the storm beside us. I have stood under nine strikes with you more times than I can count. Swear with me?"

choices.text: Swear kinship with Rowan Hale, under both skies

effects.log: You swear it under the ninth drum, his storm-vow and your old oath under the sky, and the thunder answers in a voice like rain on a roof. "Kin!" he roars, and the Marshal, of all people, bows his head.

choices.text: Tell them you would rather stay friends

effects.log: Rowan Hale nods, and does not ask again this life. "Friends," they say. "That is not small either."

choices.text: Ask what the vow means on their side

effects.log: They tell you: a name said at every hearth, a seat kept at every table, a door that is never barred. It is not so different from the east.

events.text: Rowan Hale, your sworn kin, is waiting under the cloud stair, grey-bearded, booming. "Kin!" he shouts, as if you had been gone a day. "Nine strikes. Smaller. Together."

choices.text: Stand under the storm with your sworn kin

effects.log: Shoulder to shoulder. The storm finds almost nothing to hit.

choices.text: Say his prayer over him, for once

effects.log: He goes very quiet while you say it, accent and all. "Kin," he says afterwards, gruffly. "Do not do that again. Do it every time."

events.text: The ninth strike of the ninetieth floor is the worst you have ever seen, and it is coming for you, and Rowan Hale steps under it. He raises the silver storm-sign over his head and shouts his prayer into the light, and the light takes him. When it is gone he is lying on the cloud, very still, smiling, the sign still in his fist. "Smaller," he whispers. "See? Smaller." He does not speak again.

choices.text: Carry him down the Tower yourself

effects.log: You carry him down every floor, all ninety, to the gate. The Keeper sets out a cup of tea for him, and sweeps the step where you lay him, and says, "The Tower remembers him. So will the other side." Somewhere a bell you did not ring rings once.

choices.text: Keep his storm-sign, and say his prayer

effects.log: You take the sign from his hand and say his prayer over him, every sound wrong, every word meant. Thunder answers, softly, in a voice like rain on a roof. The sign is warm in every life after this.

choices.text: Stand under the rest of the storm for him

effects.log: You stand where he stood, and the rest of the storm breaks on you and finds nothing it can move. When it clears the Marshal is kneeling beside Rowan, helm off.

events.text: At the cloud stair, where a battle-priest used to wait, there is a young priest in a grey cassock you have never met, holding a silver storm-sign worn smooth. "The Tempest Chapter sent me," the young one says. "Rowan Hale's chapter. We were told: the eastern climber he died for will come. Stand beside them. Pray the storm smaller."

choices.text: Let the young priest pray

effects.log: They pray in a voice that is not like rain on a roof yet. It will be. The storm is smaller.

choices.text: Teach them how Rowan stood

effects.log: You show them the stance, shoulder to shoulder. They learn it badly, and loudly.

events.text: Tobias Wick is on the jade stair ahead of you, and he does not wait. "Sorry," he calls back, grinning, not sorry. "The orphanage has a hundred now. I need the guardian's gift more than you do. I am climbing against you, friend. Fair and square. Mostly square." He picks the lock of the jade door and is through it before you.

choices.text: Race him, fair and square

effects.log: You race him across the jade floor and the scales, and whoever wins, he laughs, and you do too. From now on you are rivals. It suits you both better than you expected.

choices.text: Let him have this one, for the hundred

effects.log: You let him take it. He knows you did, and it makes him furious, which is how you know you are rivals now and not just friends.

choices.text: Pick his pocket on the way past

effects.log: You lift his best lockpick as he passes. He finds out three floors later and howls with delight. "Rival!" he shouts down the stairwell.

events.text: A sellsword in a good grey cloak gone shabby at the hem is resting on the landing, a black heron stitched on his shoulder: House Harrow of the Blackfen, a fallen house of his sky, he tells you, with a rueful smile. "Valen Harrow. From the other gate. I climb alone and it is dull." He walks the next floor beside you, easy company. Only once, on the stair, he asks: "What does a guardian give, exactly, when you beat it?"

choices.text: Tell him what you know of the guardians' gifts

effects.log: He listens closely, nodding, and thanks you twice. He is very good company for the rest of the floor.

choices.text: Tell him the gift is the floor, not the prize

effects.log: He laughs. "Spoken like someone whose house still has a roof," he says, lightly. You both climb on.

choices.text: Ask him why he wants to know

effects.log: "Curiosity," he says, too quickly, and then, more slowly, "my house is owed a great deal." He changes the subject. He is good at that.

events.text: Valen Harrow is waiting on the landing again, with a fire lit and bread for two. He has been a good friend these floors: he watches your back, he shares his water, he laughs at the right things. Tonight a letter lies half out of his pack, sealed with a black heron. He sees you see it and does not move to hide it.

choices.text: Read the letter while he fetches water

effects.log: It is from his house. One line is underlined twice: "Bring home a guardian's gift, by any road, or do not come home." You put it back exactly as it was.

choices.text: Leave the letter alone: it is his

effects.log: You leave it. He comes back with the water and talks about the Blackfen in spring, and you like him very much.

choices.text: Ask him about his house

effects.log: "Fallen," he says. "My father sold the last of the land to pay a debt to a better house. I am all the Harrows have left to spend." He smiles. It does not reach his eyes.

events.text: Floor after floor, Valen Harrow climbs beside you, and he has saved you twice now on the stairs. Tonight he insists on taking the second watch, and the place behind you on the stair tomorrow. When you wake in the night he is sitting very still, sharpening a short knife you have never seen him use, and looking at the stair to the guardian's door.

choices.text: Pretend to sleep, and watch him

effects.log: You watch him through your lashes until dawn. He sharpens the knife and puts it in his boot, not his belt. You will remember which boot.

choices.text: Say goodbye in the morning and climb on alone

effects.log: You tell him you will climb the next floors alone. Something crosses his face, relief or regret, and then it is gone. "Of course," he says. "Good road." You do not see him again in this life.

choices.text: Thank him for the watch, and sleep

effects.log: You sleep. In the morning he is cheerful and has breakfast ready. You climb on together, toward the guardian's door.

events.text: On the last landing below the guardian's door, Valen Harrow puts a friendly hand on your shoulder, and the other hand comes out of his boot with the short knife in it. "I am sorry," he says, and means it. "My house needs the guardian's gift more than I need a friend."

choices.text: Turn before it lands: you knew which boot

effects.log: You were watching for it. You turn, and the knife goes past your ribs into the doorframe, and you have his wrist. He stares at you. "You knew," he says. "You knew, and you climbed with me anyway." You let him go down the stairs alone.

choices.text: Take the blow, and catch him at the door

effects.log: The knife finds you. Not deep. You catch his cloak at the door anyway, and he pulls free and goes through without looking back, toward a gift he will never be able to hold. Far below, the Keeper sweeps the step where you will come down, and says, "The Tower remembers that, too."

choices.text: Take the blow, and let him go

effects.log: The knife finds you, and you let him go. He goes through the guardian's door alone. Below, at the gate, the next bell is silent for him, and you hear the Keeper say, very quietly, "That was the bargain."

events.text: A young woman with a black heron stitched on her shoulder is waiting on the landing, very straight, very pale. "Maren Harrow," she says. "Of House Harrow of the Blackfen. My uncle Valen climbed here once, and came home with a knife and no gift, and never spoke of it. Before he died he told me what he did, and to whom." She kneels. "I came to make amends for my house."

choices.text: Accept her amends, and climb a floor with her

effects.log: You raise her to her feet. You climb one floor together. At the top she bows the eastern way, carefully, as if someone had taught her. "House Harrow owes you," she says. "We will not forget it this time."

choices.text: Tell her the debt was his, not hers

effects.log: She looks up, startled. "That is not how houses work on my side," she says. "Perhaps it should be." She goes down the stairs lighter than she came.

choices.text: Refuse: some things are not mended

effects.log: She stands and bows, and does not argue. "Then House Harrow will remember that too," she says, without anger, and goes.

events.text: A knight in white mail with a pale thorn branch painted on the shield stands on the landing as if he had been waiting for you. "Aldric Vey, Knight-Commander of the Order of the Pale Thorn," he says. "My order has heard of an eastern climber who will open the door between our worlds. We do not want it opened. I am sent to stop you." He does not draw. "Not today. Today I wanted to see your face. It is fairer to hunt someone you have seen."

choices.text: Let him look, and look back

effects.log: He studies you a long moment. "Ordinary," he says, almost disappointed. "They always are." He bows and goes up the stairs ahead of you.

choices.text: Ask him why his order fears the door

effects.log: "Because what comes through a door can go both ways," he says. "Armies. Gods. Plagues. Climbers." He looks at you. "You are not an army. I will report that."

choices.text: Tell him to try, then

effects.log: He nods, unoffended. "I will," he says. "Fairly. The Order hunts with its face shown." He goes.

events.text: Aldric Vey of the Pale Thorn comes down the stair at you with his sword drawn and his face bare, as he promised, and three knights of his order behind him. "Eastern climber," he says. "In the name of the Order. Yield, or fall."

choices.text: Beat them, and spare him at the last

effects.log: You beat all four, and hold your last blow a finger from his throat, and step back. He stares at the sword you did not use. "The Order did not tell me you would do that," he says.

choices.text: Drive them back down the stair

effects.log: You drive them back floor by floor until they turn and go. "This is not over," Aldric calls up the stairwell, and it is not: the Order of the Pale Thorn will remember the eastern climber.

choices.text: Lower your weapon and tell him what the door is for

effects.log: You tell him about the bell-caster and the stonewright and a question nobody answered. His knights look at him. He lowers his sword, slowly. "Then I was sent to stop a question," he says. "I will not." His knights follow him back down.

events.text: In the storm floors Aldric Vey of the Pale Thorn is on the stair again, alone, without his order's shield. "I left them," he says. "A knight you spare is a knight you keep. I climbed to see what the door is." Then the storm comes down on you both, and he steps in front of you with his bare sword raised, and the light takes him.

choices.text: Carry him to the next landing

effects.log: He is light in his white mail. "Fair," he says at the landing, "it was fair." Then he is gone, and the Tower rings one bell you did not ring.

choices.text: Take his pale thorn badge home to his order

effects.log: You take it from his shoulder. In some life, on the other side, someone of the Pale Thorn will see it and know what he chose.

events.text: A thin mage in black feathers waits on the landing with a book open in the air beside him. "Halden Crowe, of House Crowe, the mages of the Ninefold Stair," he says. "I have read every art of my sky. I want yours. I will pay, or I will take it. I would rather pay." The book turns a page by itself, toward you.

choices.text: Teach him a little, freely

effects.log: You teach him the first breath of your art, the one every child learns. He writes it down with shaking hands. "Free," he says. "Nobody gives anything free on the Ninefold Stair." He goes away troubled.

choices.text: Refuse him

effects.log: "Then I will take it," he says, regretful, "another floor." The book snaps shut. House Crowe has marked you.

choices.text: Ask what he would do with it

effects.log: "Know it," he says. "That is all a Crowe ever wants. Then the knowing wants more." He sounds tired of himself.

events.text: Halden Crowe springs his trap on the stair: a circle of black feathers that closes round you and begins, very politely, to read your art out of you like a book. "Forgive me," he says. "House Crowe does not take no." The feathers rise.

choices.text: Break the circle and drive him off

effects.log: You break it from the inside, feather by feather, and he flees up the stair with half a page of your art and none of its heart. House Crowe will hunt the rest of it, in other skies and other lives.

choices.text: Let him read one page, and offer it as a gift

effects.log: You stop fighting and let him read one page, and tell him it is a gift. The circle falls apart in his hands. "A gift cannot be taken," he whispers. "It ruins the rite." He laughs, and it sounds like the first true laugh of his life.
